utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, before we begin, there's a matter about which the Registry wishes to clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. To clarify the exhibit numbers assigned for the documents tendered yesterday through the Witness Dmicic, the 65 ter number 1D9361 is Exhibit D3978 and 65 ter number 1D9363 is Exhibit D3979. Additionally, the transcript from yesterday has to be corrected at page 42914, line 7, it should state 12.54 and not 12.44. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Registrar. Yes, good morning, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Hamish Thomas, who is a graduate of Monash University in Australia and graduate also of Victoria University, has far too many degrees and has been extremely helpful to my team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand there is one thing on the part of the Prosecution. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President. If we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, the Defence request for presence of counsel to Defence witnesses, i.e., Mr. Popovic, Brdjanin, and Stakic, is hereby granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I don't remember the exact title of the motion. What was it? It was about Krajisnik's statement in the parliament. Can I have the expedited response from the Prosecution, in light of the fact that Krajisnik will be testifying very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You certainly may, Mr. President. Would you like it orally or in writing or -- you can have it either way you want before the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To save time, I'd like to have it in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Toholj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue? Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to look at an example of the journalism you published during your editorship of "Javnost."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter number 11957, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were editor, weren't you, in January 1991 when this was published, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is an article entitled: "The biggest slaughter of Serbs in the territory of the NDH." It's a long article which describes in detail -- and I'll just quote from the first introductory paragraph, it describes genocide conducted against Serbs in the area of Bihac, Cazinska Krajina, Bosanska Krupa, and Podgrmec. I want to read out the second paragraph, and can you see that in the B/C/S, the second paragraph which begins: "A fact from the period attracts special attention ..." Can you see that, just the on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Before we discuss the contents of this document, I just want to point out, from our perspective, this is kicking the door wide open to evidence of crimes against Serbs that you've been excluding. And if he's questioned about the credibility of his account of crimes against Serbs, then we would be -- expect to be allowed to introduce evidence of those crimes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm not going to be asking about credibility of crimes against Serbs. I'm going to be asking about the last paragraph or two of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, we've -- I've summarised it. You report crimes against Serbs during World War II. We don't need to go into any detail. What I want to draw your attention to is what you highlight in the second paragraph. "A fact from the period attracts special attention: Already in May 1941, a delegation visits Pavelic on behalf of 'the Muslims of the Bosanska Krupa district' expressing its support and loyalty, and delivers a resolution bearing 1500 signatures to him. Many of those who signed the resolution, expressing their loyalty to the greatest butcher ever to emerge from these lands, will place themselves in service of the Ustasha movement and proceed to actively participate in the ensuing days in the elimination of their neighbours, the Serbs. This is also the only possible way of explaining the mass scale of the Ustasha crimes committed in these areas. Beside those who had put on an Ustasha uniform, there were even more civilian butchers, who would receive as a reward 50 dinars each, 'a kilo of sheep's meat and a kilo of rakija' for an hour's worth of slaughtering." Do you remember that article?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would be the most powerful computer if I were able to recollect all the articles published in 1991. I don't even remember the article I read yesterday apart from the gist. And these facts that you quoted were not written here for the first time. These are citations of historical documents and books written about World War II. Or this is perhaps part of a book that was possibly published during those years, but in any case, these facts were published through trials of perpetrators of crimes during World War II, people who had been tried by the Yugoslav authorities after the war --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, we don't need to go to the detail --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And these facts emerged through trials and witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just going to refer just to a couple of extracts. I'd like you to look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Is this article authored by this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No, but he was editor of "Javnost" at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It doesn't appear to have an author -- there's an illegible author at the last page. Perhaps we can go to the very bottom of the article, you can see there's a name.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can you read the name --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I'd like to object on the grounds of relevance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's see the name first.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can you read the name at the bottom? Can you see in the last column of the piece, the name at the bottom, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm going to read out the penultimate paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Your objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, on the grounds of relevance, Mr. President. First of all, you've excluded so much of this kind of evidence about World War II throughout our Defence case. I don't think it's relevant to be used by the Prosecution. And secondly, the link between something that is published in this witness's publication versus something authored by him is so tenuous that it doesn't really make the credibility point that the Prosecution is trying to make so its probative value is extremely low even if it is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I haven't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I haven't yet asked to have this article admitted, and in my submission, the relevance of it or at least the passage that I'm about to read out will become very clear. It's about manipulation of Serbian public opinion, manipulation of the Serbian population. It's not about -- the nub of it is not about crimes committed or allegedly committed during World War II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So the penultimate paragraph, if you could look at that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And, I'm sorry, in the English it's at page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure the witness can read this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we just highlight the -- under the heading -- we can move to the top of the page in the English first, and under the heading in B/C/S: "The crime did pay off," which is the column that we see towards the bottom of the page. We can try our best to look at that. The English reads on the preceding page the heading: "The crime did pay off," and this is the text that follows.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I will read it as best I can. I'm appreciating, of course, that there is an issue with legibility. "The villages where Serbs once lived have been settled by Muslims. Thus, whether we admit it or not, it has been demonstrated that genocide is worth one's while, as far as settling, conquering living space is concerned ..." I'm leaving out the extracts which are -- appear to not be legible. "Should one then be surprised that we have such an extremely unfavourable ethnic structure here, which came to full prominence during the latest elections for new organs of authority. We would get the true statistics only if along with all the living Serbs, we were to record also their graves that which the population's natural reproduction would have brought over these last -- these barely fifty years that separate us from the beginning of the greatest crime committed against the Serb people in BiH." Now, my question to you, Mr. Toholj, is: This article, this paragraph which expresses the nub of the article, the heart of the article, which is that genocide perpetrated by Muslim civilians in league with Ustashas in World War II has been to their benefit because they settled in the villages where Serbs once lived. That's the idea that is promoted by this article, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dear lady, let me first decipher something to you. You don't have the last name of the author in the English version. His name was Nikola Zoric. I didn't know him personally, but I know he was a correspondent of the "Javnost" newspaper from this area where these crimes had happened. This point that he is making and which you are twisting, giving it a different connotation and ascribing to it a nature of propaganda which it doesn't have, was actually that wherever genocide happens, it reflects in the future numbers of population of that area. That applies to areas in Croatia, Krajina, and parts of Herzegovina. In those areas, it's natural that Serbs were killed in the areas where they lived. And I can tell you from my family history, if we are talking about history, a lot of my family had lived in Mostar were, for instance, but after 1945, there was not a single one left and they had not moved either to some other place. They were victims of crimes by the then-Independent State of Croatia; however, their property was left behind. And what happened was that the communist regime confiscated and nationalised it all. So it became nobody's property. This article is making that point, guiding people to that line of thinking; it's not propaganda. It's not geared at awakening the vengeful spirit of the Serbian people. It's not manipulation, as you interpret it. And I don't think any of the readers of "Javnost" read it the way you do. Perhaps they were more skilful readers, more used to reading historical articles.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Could I ask for that to be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- this is not written by the -- this witness, and then is it your position that editor-in-chief is monitoring or proofreading its correspondents' writing? It's allegedly Nikola Zoric's report and that its editor-in-chief is in one way or another related to this report?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Responsible for content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? I should only like to ask, is the Prosecution trying to say that this is false propaganda and that these things did not happen in World War II? That is a different matter, and if this is so, then the Defence is faced with different tasks. They should just make it plain: Is this a lie or is it the truth? And if it is the truth, then what is wrong with publishing it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we make the decision, would you like to respond to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I've made the position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- plain. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has doubt about its relevance, Ms. Pack. Further, we note that the relevant passages have been read out in the transcript, so there's no need to admit it. So the Chamber will not admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: During the war, one of your roles as minister for information was to provide misleading information about crimes against Bosnian Muslims and Croats, to deny crimes against Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not one of my roles. The task of the minister of information in every government where it exists, and in war time such ministries usually exist, is to play a kind of logistics for the government system that the state controls in one way or another, and even over private media, which in war time was not our case very often. So my role was not to falsify events, to adapt or change the facts relating to current developments, but to provide logistical support from legal logistics to such requirements as keeping a certain number of reporters, cameramen, et cetera, in television studios and save them from being mobilised. So it was more of a logistical role than a manipulative one.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, you continue to manipulate, to deny the commission of crimes against Bosnian Muslims and Croats today, don't you? Let me just refer you to paragraph 87 of your statement and the interview that you talk about in there, 20th January 2006 in Svedok.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have that up. It's 1D9051. I think it's now been exhibited, but I don't have the number, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may ask the Trial Chamber's leave to let the witness have a hard copy of his statement in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary, we'll do so but --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: He doesn't need it quite yet. We can just have the article up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, you tell us in your statement and I can read it to you directly, you say that this article still reflects your views; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes, but this interview was taken by telephone, and I never received a copy for authorisation. And I know that I was very unhappy when it was published because I like to authorise texts of my interviews in advance for purposes of precision. It reads rather different than what I would write personally, but to a great extent it does reflect my views.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, we'll go, please, to the English at page 2 and the B/C/S, please, at page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'll just read you a quick passage and then we'll go over to page 3. Talking about Srebrenica. You say there at the second response, bottom of the paragraph about Srebrenica: "The culmination of the myth of Serbian guilt and Serbian criminality was Srebrenica. The story of Srebrenica begins before all the stories about the war in BH and ends after all the stories about that war." So you're talking about Srebrenica. And I want to go to the following page, please, in both languages, as you elaborate. You can see in the middle of the page your response: "Based on what facts do you claim that there was no genocide in Srebrenica?" And here are the facts that you state in your article, in your interview: "In Srebrenica there were individual cases of revenge, but there was no genocide. After the Muslim 28th Division broke out from Srebrenica, a parade of that unit was held in Tuzla. In this footage, we were able to see many who later appeared on the lists of persons killed. Not a single woman or child was killed there, which clearly shows that there was no genocide. 3.000 'dead' people in Srebrenica got up to vote in the elections in Tuzla. All the civilians arrived in Kladanj and Tuzla. The Prosecution in The Hague is aware of this, and that is why they are avoiding a discussion about Srebrenica, while they reach agreements with the accused or force them to confess. The claims by the Muslims that the victims are civilians because of their clothing and not soldiers are also dubious. I have a copy of a document that clearly shows that one of the commanders in charge of security for the Srebrenica division said that it was not good that a local radio station was talking about how aid sent by Indonesia in the form of sports shoes was being distributed to soldiers." Then your concluding sentence says: "Following the liberation of Srebrenica and Zepa, 1.200 Muslim combatants fled to Serbia. Although they later went to third countries with the help of international humanitarian organisations, they are also listed as victims from Srebrenica." All lies; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are all facts, Madam, that I stand behind. The document which is mentioned here exists; I have it in my files. I can send it to you privately or officially. And another thing, by contrast to you, I know where Trnovo and Kladanj are located, I know where Srebrenica and Bajina Basta are located, and you cannot say that someone who was killed in Srebrenica was killed there if he was killed in Trnovo because between Srebrenica and Trnovo the distance is 50 or 60 kilometres and it's very difficult terrain to cross over --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This doesn't talk about the Trnovo killings and I want to talk to you about the numbers. Now, you deny here, you deny the mass execution of thousands of Muslim men after the fall of Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would ask the Chamber to ask Madam Prosecutor not to raise her voice while questioning me because there is no need for that. The facts speak for themselves. So I do not deny -- a little while ago I did not deny anything. I just said that between Srebrenica, Trnovo and Kladanj, the distances are 50 or 60 kilometres and that there are other settlements in between, so there is no continuity. It's not one settlement. It's not Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Pause, Mr. Toholj --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it's, let's say, Eastern Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We don't need to focus on the geography, on the half truth. I'm asking you about the numbers. Thousands of men were executed after the fall of Srebrenica. My question to you: Do you deny that truth? Do you deny those facts?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And do you assert and claim what you just said? Can you stand behind it? In my public appearances on TV and in my many appearances in front of large numbers of audience, I kept advocating one argument. Each man had their single identification number with residence, date of birth, and so on. So what I advocate is that this should be established. Each man is an entity, a cosmos, a being. So you cannot put several thousand people into a phrase about several thousand people who are killed. One killed person, that's already a crime. Why doesn't anyone ever accept this argument that the victims should be put in their place one by one, establishing the date of birth, the date of death, the circumstances under which the death came, and not to put all people who were killed in Podrinje in Potocari whenever --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Toholj, why aren't you answering my question? My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's deal with specific questions one by one. In the article, Mr. Toholj, you said: "3.000 'dead' people in Srebrenica got up to vote in the election of Tuzla." 3.000 voted in the election. Where did you base this statement, "3.000 'dead' people voted in Tuzla"? Do you have the statistics with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have it here on me, but I will refer you to the book of Ms. Diana Johnstone, The crazy war against Yugoslavia, the crazy NATO war against Yugoslavia, where she presents the evidence that a certain number of people were killed and then a number of Muslims, Bosniaks, from Srebrenica turned up on the lists of missing persons and then this number was multiplied twice. I don't remember literally the argument, but it's presented in the book. Diana Johnstone is a relevant author internationally and I was referring to that source --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where did Ms. Diana Johnstone get those statistics, that 3.000 allegedly dead people voted in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She referred to the research that she did on the basis of documents of the ICRC and some other documents, and as for her book, I bought the copyright for the Serbian language and I published it as a publisher. I don't remember all the data. It's not all fresh in my memory at the moment, so I couldn't answer more specifically. Of course, the purpose of this article, or rather, this interview is not to diminish the number of the people who perished in Srebrenica, the Bosniaks who perished, but to refer -- or, rather, to invite a detailed research of everything that happened, not only in Srebrenica but in all of Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout the war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Toholj, could you be as brief as possible in answering the question. One more point that I can't follow in your statement is that The Hague -- The Hague is avoiding a discussion about Srebrenica. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wanted to say precisely what -- similar to something that I said a while ago. It avoids -- not ICTY, but the OTP avoids discussing Srebrenica in the manner which I only believe to be solid and serious, and that is to take each man as an object of crime or a victim of crime and then establish all the circumstances, from the name, the DNA, and whatever else, the address, the place of birth, the place of execution, the place of death, so that the Bosniak victims from Kladanj cannot be ascribed to Srebrenica. So that's already where the grain of manipulation has been sowed with the myth of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to understand your manipulations. Paragraph 87 of your statement you say to us -- you state that: "At the Vatican, one day after the liberation of Srebrenica, I saw that the Western printed media were writing that genocide had been committed in Srebrenica; therefore, this was as early as 12 July 1995. This was a great surprise for me. Everyone that we talked to at the Vatican told us that a terrible crime had been committed in Srebrenica, although the military operation had only just been completed. Therefore, this media campaign that had been prepared in advance was launched immediately and this is still going on today. My impression was that the purpose of this campaign was to weaken the negotiating position of the Serbian side in the talks that were to be held in Geneva and later in Dayton." Can you help me understand what exactly you are stating there, Mr. Toholj? Is your claim that the Western printed media were writing that genocide in Srebrenica -- were writing about genocide in Srebrenica as early as 12 July and that this, therefore, proves that the media campaign had been prepared in advance? Is that the point you're making?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the substance, but I would only correct the date. I think that I had a slip of the tongue. I meant the 13th to the 14th, because on the 12th I had arrived in Rome, and I brought and handed over to the Defence team, the front page of "Corriere della Sera" where there is an article that stated that genocide had been committed. And in all the talks with cardinals and other high officials of the Catholic church, we received information and accusations. There were no questions. They knew undoubtedly that a horrible crime had happened there, and as "Corriere della Sera" reported, the crime was one of genocide. So it was a campaign - there were campaigns about rapes of Bosniak women in Bosnia conducted in the same manner - when in a number of media, the printed press and the TV stations and so on, simultaneously one and the same topic is reported about and, of course, the perpetrator is also the same for whatever is mentioned as having been committed. So it did sound as a joint accusation of Serbs for something that we didn't know anything about as yet, except for what I learned later on from a report of the Dutch Defence Ministry, a report that was made on the basis of the debriefing with all members of the DutchBat in Srebrenica; namely, that the military operation in Srebrenica was conducted perfectly in the military sense of the word, precisely with few troops, and that no crimes --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Wait --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- had been committed. That was the only thing that could be known by that date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Slip of the tongue, I think you refer to the date, 12th of July, which you have in your statement here that you signed, as a slip of the tongue. You, the writer, the propagandist, you mistakenly identified the onset of the Western printed media campaign as 12 July in your statement; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I did not write this article. I was giving an interview on the telephone. I was not even located in Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm talking about your statement --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- please let me explain -- it wasn't me who made a mistake about the date, it was -- yes, then it was a slip of the tongue. But on the 12th, there were already objections that something had happened in Srebrenica, something awful about which I in Rome, even though I did not participate in military operations ever and anywhere, should feel guilty that my negotiating position -- or, rather, during our talks in Vatican, whatever we discussed in the talks, our position was much weaker than it should have been. And of course, the wish was to weaken the negotiating position of the Serbs at a higher level, primarily that was the idea. And I stand by the claim that the date is not so important, whether it's the 12th or the 13th, but if it's the 12th, then it was on the 12th. I made a report for our government organs, for the president of the republic, the prime minister, and I stated all the details in it. It's a report on the delegation's stay in Vatican.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, the date is important, isn't it? And I'd like to refer you to one of your more incredible lies.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: If we look at 65 ter 25460A, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is -- while we're waiting for the English, this is a speech that you gave at the scientific meeting "Vojislav Seselj's concept of defence at The Hague Tribunal." And it's extracted from Seselj's book, the title of which I won't read out, published in 2006 -- given in 2006, this speech. You remember giving a speech within this context in 2006 in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember I gave a number of speeches in this framework in terms of this subject, but at the moment I can't see this speech of mine in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to the following page in B/C/S. We need to go to page 2 in the B/C/S, please, and we need to go to page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm just going to read a couple of extracts. We'll just start with the bottom of this page just to put things in context. You're talking about July 1995 in this speech.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And we can go, in fact, over to the following page, page 3, both in English and also in B/C/S. Bottom of the page in the English and in the B/C/S about halfway down.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's just beginning with the -- in the paragraph beginning: "Pope Satan landed not just in Sarajevo after the war, when a hunting season on Serbian leaders in Bosnia opened, but also in Banja Luka." We've got that paragraph; right? Go about halfway down into it, where it begins: "In the Vatican at the time ..." Perhaps if you follow, you'll see your speech there in writing. This is what you say: "In the Vatican at that time, one day after the liberating of Srebrenica, this is the essence of what I am saying, our envoys spoke to various ranking officials of the papal government, including Monsignor Monterisi, the French Archbishop Charles, and a few other Swiss assistants to the foreign minister. Yet all of them, what a holy providence, already knew in advance what happened in an Eastern Bosnian Kasaba and who liquidated who, to the number. The next day already, a glorious Serbian military operation was described as a crime forever overshadowing the Jasenovac crimes and all other Nazi and Fascist crimes in World War II. Let me note that the Western press and television were a few days behind the Vatican monsignori. These were followed and caught up with by the same ones," going over the page in English, "by the same ones trying to convince the people in Serbia that the last decade of the 20th century was marked by Serbian crimes. "The climax of such Vatican forgeries came, as we all know, in 1999 ..." and so it continues. Do you remember giving that speech?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I remember, but I would like you to explain to me why do you believe -- what is a lie here?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Here you appear to be claiming - perhaps you can help us - you appear to be claiming that the execution of thousands of Muslim men after the fall of Srebrenica is a Vatican forgery; is that your claim? That actually -- doesn't that actually summarise the lie you were seeking to propagate within the paragraph I have read out?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, it is your lie that I want to say that. No. I wanted to say exactly what I did say, and it's my writer's impression summarised into a speech which should be easy for a great mass of people, the listeners who were present in this hall at the time. And the fact that I said for the Pope that he was the devil, it's of equal value if someone said that he were a saint. It is my personal impression that I'm entitled to. And as for the Vatican monsignori, the two of them are mentioned here, said that a horrible crime had happened in Srebrenica and had been committed by the Serbs. It was a campaign because absolutely there was no -- even no reports from news agencies that would have been detailed or established on facts, and they already had that. So if you take into account the fact that Pope John Paul II, or Pope Wojtyla, as he is a Polish man, advocated the policies during the war and how the Serbs should be punished after Dayton, and the fact that he visited not only Sarajevo but Banja Luka, and how he established that a man who participated in crimes that you presented to me through Zoric's report, turn him into a saint, it was a campaign and nothing more than that. It's not a lie, it's an impression, which I still have and which I still feel inside when I think about my visit to Vatican.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to have the pages, at least the front page and the page from which I've read -- pages from which I've read admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Exhibit Number P6488, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is 2006, isn't it, that you give this speech? 2006?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I would give a similar speech or a speech like this even today, and I will probably publish it in one of my books, diaries, or something, the words that I spoke on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me be clear, Mr. Toholj. What you are saying here is that you heard about genocide from Vatican as to what happened in Srebrenica at the time of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I first received information verbally, not from Vatican, but from the people we met then and they were the officials of the Vatican State. And then later on in the hotel, in the city of Rome, I bought the newspapers and on the first pages were those articles on the front page of "Corriere della Sera," although I can't really read Italian, but I understand a few words via Latin, genocide was mentioned. So that was the first knowledge that I ever had about the happenings in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that that article referred to the killing of thousands of Muslims at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, I don't think that I said or claimed that. I said that the title of the article -- I couldn't even have read the article. I read and understood the title. And as for the thousands -- I know how you say "thousands" in Italian, but I did not read the entire article, but the title itself was speaking enough for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's enough. You didn't read the content of the article. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's not just what you say in this speech, though, is it? You say, and I'll quote again: "All of them -- all of them already knew in advance what happened in an Eastern Bosnian Kasaba and who liquidated who, to the number," that's what you're stating there, isn't it, that when you were in the Vatican, these people, these monsignori knew in advance what then took place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't in advance then. It was parallel with the events. But no news agencies had processed that, there was no information, no data, and they knew that horrible massacres had happened and that the Serbs had committed them, not specific Serbs by first and last names or such and such a unit or group or paramilitaries, but Serbs, generally speaking, so that our ears hurt. Because for 20 years we have been listening to the same sort of accusation: The Serbs did it. And here at this Tribunal you claim that crime is always personalised and should be seen as such and proved and sentenced. And still when anyone is speaking and presenting this, you always say: The Serbs, and it was so there at the time. And that reinforced the impression which I stated at this scientific gathering devoted to Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: In 2006, of course, you would have been well aware of the report of the RS government commission for investigation of the events in and around Srebrenica between 10th and 19th July 1995. That's the title of the report that was issued in 2004; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not quite understand. What was it that was published in 2004?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: An RS government commission report.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: P06220, if we can have that up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I just want to read you a conclusion in this report. You can look at page 32 in the English and B/C/S page 39, please. RS government commission concluded, and you can see there, it's the second point in the B/C/S and English on this page, concluded that it was: "Established that between the 10th and 19th July 1995, several thousands of Bosniaks were liquidated in a manner that represents severe violation of international humanitarian law, and that the perpetrators, among others, undertook measures to cover up the crime by relocating the bodies." You can't dismiss this as a Vatican forgery or Western media propaganda, can you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer, I'm going to ask you kindly to show me who the members of this commission were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We're not going to go into any detail. We're not going to look at the members of the commission. You can deal with that in re-examination if necessary. Deny -- you deny the accuracy of these findings, that several thousands were liquidated, several thousands of Bosniaks were liquidated?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, may I answer your previous question? It is very important who the members of the commission were because I know that one of the members of this commission that collaborated this report is Mr. Smail Cekic, who, in 1994, ten years before this event, published a book in Sarajevo: "Genocide over the Bosniaks." So much about genocide, so much for the members of the commission. And now let me respond to your question. This is an extorted document in a classical political way that you or whoever is going to put to a Serb, in this courtroom or anywhere else, as undeniable evidence of genocide. So that is to say the matter is adjudicated as far as Srebrenica is concerned --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Toholj, pause, please --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I actually never read this --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We're getting to the answer to the question, I hope. Can you answer my question?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My haven't read this text and I do not stand by this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Toholj, we'll move on. You continued to correspond with Dr. Karadzic when he was a fugitive; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: In March 2002, you launched with Kosta Cavoski the web site for the committee for the truth about Radovan Karadzic. You were the secretary of the committee; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we established an NGO, an association, consisting of some 50 or 60 people. It was of international nature. These were reputable people. The exact name of this NGO, this association, was the International Committee for the Truth about Radovan Karadzic. It is correct that we also had our own web site and we presented to the public part of the material that we had through that web site.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have P06291, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is a letter from your book: "Night post correspondence with Radovan Karadzic," which you published in 2008. This is a letter from Radovan Karadzic to you dated October 2001, to you, Miroslav.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We'll go to the second page, please. Thank you. Just take it up, please, the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: "I'm glad that the material for the web site is slowly building up," that's the web site you set up; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And then it goes on, it talks about Srebrenica. "This is really the only place where something evil happened, but it can clearly be seen where it was thought up and who carried it out ..." It goes on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Just take it up, please, at the bottom paragraph there. "I am sending you these disks that Ljiljana gathered. On the ones I'm sending you, I deleted all that I thought should not go (I saved the originals) but there might be more reductions necessary. I trust that you will review each report and make a decision on it yourself ..." It goes on, skip a couple of sentences. "I kept a couple of speeches from the Assembly (I deleted the others) some of whom are a dramatic testimony about what was happening to us or what those brothers did to us, or the foreigners or our soldiers. Of course, I did not mention our worst disgraces, but I do think that some of the things that disgrace us, up to an acceptable level, should be published. I was particularly careful of not jeopardising anyone. I also got rid of anything that would jeopardise," going over the next page, "anyone or that would look like a non-gentlemanly stone-throwing at Slobodan or his prime minister ..." And then if we just skip to the last page, please, page 6 of the English. And similarly, page 4 in the B/C/S, the last page. I'd like to take it up, the penultimate -- I apologise, it's the fourth paragraph up. "I am sending you the disks now from which, unless you deem otherwise, all can be uploaded onto the site. I'll then send you the 'statements and appeals' ..." and so on, it goes on. "What remains after that are the documents registered under 'mercy documents' which I will collect and sort out shortly. Those are mostly abolitions, releases of POWs who were an obstruction to us anyway, one-sided cease-fires, et cetera. I am not sure whether their place is on the site, you will assess it yourself ..." and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is how you, Mr. Toholj, you the propagandist, put together the web site for the committee for the truth about Radovan Karadzic; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not entirely right because at that time I was not very computer literate and I could not update a computer web site, but I did edit the content of the web site at my desk. Our motto was that everything, even the facts that are not in favour of Radovan Karadzic, should be on the web site and should be made accessible. So our task, our objective, our decision was not to hide anything because we thought that nothing should be hidden, that everything should be known, that everything should be accessible to the public and for history. What is written in the letter of my friend -- and you know that private letters have a special kind of jargon that is close to the jargon that is used in love. I believe that you expect that part of the material is missing after this sentence and that this has to do with something sensational that is unpleasant -- that could be unpleasant for the public. No. No. This just has to do with what is being repeated several times because the president told different media the same things several times, so we wanted to avoid this kind of duplication, not to burden the web site with all of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This jargon that you describe is a process of manipulation, isn't it, manipulation of the historical record; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a historical record. Jargon of love in letters and the like, if one can speak of manipulation, but I don't think it's manipulation. I think it is encouragement, spurring on some positive feelings, and how can you link something that is so stupid up to me after my 15 books were praised very highly by critics?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You're aware, aren't you, Mr. Toholj, that documents went missing in 1997 and 1998 from the presidential archives in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know because on the basis of a decision made by the high representative of the international community, I can't remember what it was called exactly, Mr. Carlos Westendorp, I was dismissed from work and I was forbidden from doing anything, from working as such. And quite simply, I was told that there was no place for me whatsoever, and it was then that I moved to Belgrade straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, we'll look at the period after you were dismissed from work. You were aware of an investigation into the missing archives in 2004 carried out by the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have, please, 65 ter 25234.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: See if this helps you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Part of this has been admitted as P6398, but I'm going to look at another portion. Second page, please, in both languages. This is a report into that investigation and I'm going to ask to look, please, at page 14 of the English, page 11 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This report posits a theory and I want to ask you about that, a few theories. One of the theories, paragraph 5, is that, and you can see that in your language --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: In fact, forgive me. It's at page 10 of the B/C/S. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: One of the theories is that, we see at point 5: "Part of the documentation reached the territory of the Republic of Serbia and is being used by the Committee for the Defence of Radovan Karadzic for writing their books and documents. "There is an objective possibility that people close to Radovan Karadzic had moved a part of the documentation from the offices of the Presidency to the territory of Serbia." And then we can just go down to the following page in the English and point 2 of the following text in -- on page 11 in the B/C/S. It says -- I'll just read it. Again, two versions of outcomes of the investigation, two theories. Second version, point 2, is: "... that in the 1996-1998 period, people close to Radovan Karadzic or his security moved the documentation from the official premises of the Presidency to a certain passive location, and that they gave a part of the documentation to the Committee for the Defence of Radovan Karadzic, headed by Kosta Cavoski, who was using the documentation for writing the books and articles related to Radovan Karadzic." And then the following page, 16, in the English you are asked, and just going down a bit the page in the B/C/S: "We contacted the Republika Srpska MUP," you can see there, "for a second time with the aim of securing a witness interview with the writer," and so on, "Cavoski," and just take up with you, "as well as with writer Miroslav Toholj, who wrote a book ..." et cetera, "which lists the copies of original documents of the said archive." I'm paraphrasing there. Do you know anything about that? Were you contacted for an interview, an interview about the missing archives?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I've never seen this document. I was not aware of its existence. I see that there is a lot of speculation there as far as I'm concerned. I don't know why the minister stopped at this. No one ever talked to me about archives. From a friend, I received information from Banja Luka to the effect that the newspapers published a piece saying that carloads of material were taken away from me. That was not published. I could speak about that at length. I don't know anything about this, in short. You saw from the letter that President Karadzic sent to me that not paper is referred to but disks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd ask for the pages to which I've referred to be admitted in evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we add it to the Exhibit P6398?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 13, Mr. Toholj said the search was not carried out. Here it says "published," "objavljen," "objavljen," so it didn't say that this search was carried out on behalf of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Toholj? Do you confirm having said so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did not quite understand what the correction was. I stated a moment ago that no one talked to me about the missing documentation, no one ever talked to me about that. If so, perhaps there is a record and then my denial can be refuted; then afterwards, after this date, a search was conducted in my apartment, the house that was being built, and then the warehouse of the publishing house, et cetera. There are proper records that were printed at the end of this book containing everything that was found when this search was conducted. So there is no mention of this, not a single object of this report was found on me, whatever this document may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: In 1997/1998, you still had access, didn't you, to the archives for SRT, yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were personally involved, weren't you, in 1997 and 1998, in the removal and destruction of material considered unfavourable to the accused; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we take a look at 65 ter 23489A.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, this is a letter that we have only in English, and I'm going to have to read it out to you and you can listen to the translation. It is a letter from Milos Vukasinovic to Dr. Karadzic dated the 6th of February, 1998. It's about a visit that Tribunal investigators made a third --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. Could the witness please see the original, in the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we have translation for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This document hasn't been translated and it wasn't made available in the Serbian language in the first instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. But I way -- but what is an SRT? Is it --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: My apologies for --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can identify SRT is Serbian Radio and Television; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is the -- this is the state-owned TV company in the RS during the war?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Radio TV network with several stations, not a station.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Serbian Radio and Television; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Serbian Radio and Television.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon, may I just ask, the original, did Milos Vukasinovic write this in English? Why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- should there be a translation from this English into Serbian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll discuss it in -- when Ms. Pack tenders this document or you can deal with it in your cross or whatever, but this is not a proper time, after having heard that Ms. Pack has no B/C/S translation or original.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm going to take this up halfway down the document and I'm going to read it in English. It's about the OTP, Office of the Prosecutor, visit. "They were mostly interested in the SDS documentation until May of 1992 and crisis/emergency centres. They paid special attention to reporting/informing of medias, particularly television. At the same time these two issues represent a threat. By examining the documentation which Duvnjak has, I am convinced that there are documents that present danger. I suggested to Vrkes to call the SDS Presidents from certain municipalities in the eastern part due to undertaking activities to remove or destroy specific documents related to field work/terrain. He said that he will make contact with you in regards to the above stated ..." It goes on a bit and then just going over the page: "A certain 'Nancy' was in Zvornik and Bijeljina this week and last week she told Neskovic that she is interested in that type of documentation. The Tribunal representatives were in TV today and asked for all your statements as well as all news for the time-period related to the events in Srebrenica dated 1995. Maybe I am scared by nature, however, I think that all your statements are not really favourable. I will state an example. In May of 1992, you stated that there is work and law in the Republic of Srpska and that everything is in normal order and that the Muslim part is in a chaos. However, our defence strategy for that time-period is that the chaos was there. They gave specific requests to TV, and with Toholj we need to check and evaluate the significance of these statements. As a matter of fact, we need to do some good thinking for TV ..." You were involved, weren't you in the process of reviewing these archives and TV and removing anything deemed unfavourable to Dr. Karadzic, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, that is indeed a major lie on your part. Your investigator came to see me and you could have heard from him what happened during his visit. I was asked to allow this investigator to review the archives. We did not know what he was interested in, we did not know what he would be looking for. He had a man assigned to help him. I did that. They did not even look for written material. They just looked for video material. He went to a room and he recorded everything that he might have been interested in. Nothing more than that. I don't remember his name. You must know his name. I don't think I even knew his name at the time. He went there, he recorded all of that. You can check what he found there. After all, you do know, but you are taking advantage of my lack of information in order to pin this on me, namely, this assertion that I took part in the destruction of material. You know, from my point of view, to destroy a metre or a second of video material that can no longer -- that cannot be restored is a crime against history and I would never take part in anything like that. As director-general, I kindly allowed your investigator to go to the archives and to record things that he deemed necessary for your purposes. I wasn't even interested in what it was that he had recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So you say you didn't help the accused's associates in giving them access to the TV archives so that they could review those archives, remove anything unfavourable to the accused?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who would ever ask me? And I didn't. Such a request was never made, and even if it had been made I would not have done it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I would like to admit this document, please. We spoke about it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- I will follow that up. Any objections, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I know we don't have the original, but you've dealt with this issue before, similar letters from the same individual and admitted them. So I think the same ruling would apply and the lack of original would go to the weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure this should be -- I'll leave it at that. Mr. Toholj, we'll adjourn -- we'll have a break and resume at five past 11.00. Could you excuse yourself first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll receive it. Shall we assign a number for this?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document receives Exhibit Number P6489, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we have 65 ter 21582, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This, Mr. Toholj, I'm going to give you an opportunity to read. It's a reply from Dr. Karadzic to Milos Vukasinovic dated 8th February 1998 to the letter we just saw, that I just read to you. I'd like to read it to you, please. "Dear Milos," and I'll just pick it up second sentence. "I think you personally have done a lot. If it's just removing the necessary, it's a lot. Please keep going in that direction. I don't understand how they in the Ministry of Defence were not smart enough to take care of everything on time." Next paragraph: "Please do not allow such a mistake to repeat itself with the Television. You ought to personally review every segment which will be offered to them and select those favourable to us and detrimental to the Muslims. Nothing else exists because the archives have been moved, destroyed, and so forth. If necessary, determine the associates from the TV and the costs, that is, the fees, in order to have everything reviewed before it's offered to them. There should be nothing else outside of that which you will have reviewed." Next paragraph: "You are completely right when it comes to the SDS as well." Skipping a sentence. "The best would be if the archives did not exist at all because the party was frozen for a year." And I'll just pick it up with the media again, the following sentence. "There are also some great statements of mine in Javnost and other media. There is a statement that was published this year, reprinted from some Belgrade newspapers, an interview ..." and it goes on. And then just taking it up at the bottom of the page in English: "There are many statements to go to my and our advantage. Everything else needs to be darkened out, it doesn't exist. You know that sometimes journalists themselves would escalate and radicalise statements, and the times were such that we could not tone them down or deny. "Invite Vrkes to come and see you, show him this letter, and tell him about our contacts, have him do everything - in person, not through telephone or letter - to have the archives in municipalities cleared out so they wouldn't go to hell or some of them wouldn't be pursued for a trifle or not to spoil what's being worked on centrally." And I'll just pick it up where you're mentioned in the next-but-one paragraph. "Give my regards to Toholj and ask him on my behalf to allow you to review everything that is to be offered to them, and you choose your co-workers maybe from the TV and we'll pay them. "I don't think we should facilitate or encourage their plotting and scheming any further. They have received that which we too were interested in and now we should be discretely obstructing them except on TV but there too we should only give what serves our purpose." And just the bottom two sentences: "I think we have been very obliging. Now we should take stock and obstruct. The more good documents and less bad ones they have, the easier it will be for them to work in our favour. And our friends will find it easier to justify their moves in our favour, if the ratio of documents is far more to our advantage." So you were aware, weren't you, that Dr. Karadzic was communicating to Milos Vukasinovic in this vein regarding the review so far as you're concerned of the TV archives to remove anything considered to be unfavourable to the accused?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't understand at all on the basis of what are you claiming that I was privy to this correspondence?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Are you claiming then that Milos Vukasinovic didn't follow-up with you as instructed by Dr. Karadzic in this letter?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am claiming that Milos Vukasinovic did not pass on to me the greetings sent by Mr. Karadzic in this letter. I assert that Milos Vukasinovic did not enter a single video or audio archive of the Serbian Radio and Television. And I should like know if you know of all the places where the archives were stored, the archives that Milos Vukasinovic and even your people could access and review. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I don't answer questions.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, then --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to have this document admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document receives Exhibit Number P6490, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You would agree with me, wouldn't you, Mr. Toholj, that this is -- letter indicates a process of obstructing of ICTY investigators in their investigations?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, that would be my pre-conclusion, but I'm here to testify about facts. I will answer the question that I posed to you. The archives of the Serbian Radio and Television was in all the studios within the network, in Trebinje, Pale, Banja Luka, and Prijedor, and Bijeljina. So physically, one person within a short period of time, even three or five people, any number up to ten, could not review the entire archive because you know that the television broadcasts 24 hours a day, but the original programme is broadcast 10 to 12 hours per day. That's a huge amount of material which was physically impossible to review, and it's absolutely absurd to expect that it could be combed in some way in order to be censored. And finally, there was no need because all of that had already been broadcast somewhere and anybody was able to make a copy on a VCR. All of that was public. Those were not secret documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm aware I've got five more minutes and I've got one matter which I can deal with in five minutes, and there's a further matter which just arose out of a question about SRT earlier which I can deal with in about six or seven minutes which would be in addition to the time I have left. So my request is -- is for leave to have that additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm very grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I want to ask you about another letter from Dr. Karadzic, this time to you, 65 ter 24910B. This was published in your book: Correspondence, again, night post, conducted while he was a fugitive. It's a letter dated the 27th of October, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And I'd ask, please, to go to page 19 of the English and in the B/C/S page 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It starts -- this is a letter -- you would agree this is a letter from Dr. Karadzic to you, yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Oh, it's not up yet. It's 24910B. And then in the B/C/S it's page 24 in e-court and in the English it's page 19.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is after you have been removed from your position as general-manager of Serbian Radio and Television in 1997; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And second paragraph: "I hope your people are well." You've got a footnote and you're referring to the editors and journalists at Srpska Radio and Television, SRT, so those are your people at SRT. Just taking it up a couple of sentences down: "I think you should keep your people together, let them keep making the Dnevnik as if nothing has happened, one copy for history and the rest for the local television stations, which should be delivered to them halfway by courier. I have been informed that we could start again soon, at least in one specific area, plus the local televisions. I suggested to V. O.," that's Velibor Ostojic, yes? Your predecessor as minister of information? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: "I suggested to V. O. to let N. L. work with Sveti Jovan," that's Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic's daughter Sonja's radio station, "and make news broadcasts, short ones, to be aired every hour and leave the longer news for Dnevnik-type broadcast," et cetera. "The news, thus edited, could be sent by fax to every local television station that wants to broadcast". And then he says: "Speaking about the new company," and this is the new company that Velibor Ostojic had set up, isn't it, the news agency --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we turn to the next page for the witness in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I thank you, Dr. Karadzic, for -- next page. "Speaking about the new company," it says, in your footnote there, the new media centre you're talking about there is the news editorial office, aren't you, that was established by Velibor Ostojic in this period?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a reference to that, but as far as I know that centre remained an idea. It was never put into practice. We never succeeded in breaking through the media blockade with that joint venture with mixed equity, but as far as I know the idea was never translated into practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And it goes into some detail about what to do regarding this. Just taking it up at the bottom of the page in the English: "Therefore, as you will see in the letter which I have sent to V. O., I thought I would make the following combination ..." It goes into some detail thereafter on the following page. Next: "We could give it a neutral name and present some completely unknown persons as the formal editor and director, to manage until the elections and the following year ..." and so on. It says: "I am asking you at the end to study these reasons and meet with N. L. and V. O, then you can decide what is best."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Then just jumping to the last page in the English and also the last page in the B/C/S, yes, 26 in e-court, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It starts: "Please don't let the party committee, the one that you're in, sag away," that's the commission for information and propaganda that we spoke about yesterday; right? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's obviously a reference to the commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: "One should go to every house before the elections with at least five or six leaflets. It is not enough to read them to the local and municipal SDS boards, they have to enter every house, but in a way that it doesn't let them punish us" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have the correct page?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It seems to have skipped forward in English to the next letter. It should be in the English at page 20. My apologies. It's just the last paragraph of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And it says: "One should go to every house before the elections, with at least five or six leaflets. It is not enough to read them to the local and municipal SDS boards, they have to enter every house ..." et cetera. Signed Radovan. This modus operandi we see spoken about here in the last paragraph, this was the means by which the SDS operated before and during the war, wasn't it, to ensure contact by SDS local boards with every Serbian house?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you again linked up two things that cannot be connected. This is a reference here to the election campaign which the Serbian Democratic Party entered under a great pressure from international players without its leader who was forced to go into hiding. It was decimated. In many municipalities, very hard-working and serious people were prevented from running. So everything had been done at that moment for the SDS to lose at the elections, and the quest was for a Western-type democracy allegedly. And in those circumstances, we were trying to inform the people as best we could. In the media blockade, all the transmitters we had had been disabled by IFOR and we were deprived of any possibility of presenting our views so something had to be done. And as far as I know in Serbia and anywhere else where elections are held, it is quite normal for flyers to be placed in mailboxes everywhere, to present information about their candidates. So I don't see anything in this that is different from widely accepted international practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Even when Dr. Karadzic was a fugitive, you and Velibor Ostojic continued to communicate with him on matters related to the control of the media in the RS; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not control of the media because we were not in control of all the media at that time. On the contrary, every party had under its control a couple of radio stations, a couple of TV stations, although the smaller ones were mainly concentrated in Banja Luka. Other parties had their own independent newspapers which had been started up even before this. There were other media outlets started and financed by political parties. We had some influence on one radio station, one media centre in Bijeljina which was very soon afterwards destroyed by explosives, otherwise our voice was not heard. And as to the part of your question which has to do with our contact with Mr. Karadzic, yes, we had contact with him at that time, and sometime in that period Velibor Ostojic died.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can I have that document admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit those pages together with the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Just the whole of the letter of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- the 27th October. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This receives the document -- the Exhibit Number P6491, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Since we've referred to correspondence with Velibor Ostojic, I just want to take you very quickly to one such letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And that is 65 ter 25465. I just want to have, please, page 2 in the English, B/C/S page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Addressed: "Dear Velibor," it's to Velibor Ostojic. It's from Dr. Karadzic. It doesn't state his name at the end. You can agree with me, when you read it, that it's from Dr. Karadzic. 12th October 1997. And I just want to take it up just on the second page in the English. The paragraph in the B/C/S that reads about halfway down the page: "The biggest reason for me writing to you is the media. I have already said what should be done. Now I repeat, start with 'Javnost' as soon as possible and turn 'Oslobodjenje' into a daily and shortly afterwards, through additional capital, turn it into an independent paper, just as the Turks did. 'Javnost' through additional capital should be returned to the Party ..." et cetera. And then your area: "Until we get our day back at SRT or until we get a different channel, we are left with local municipal radio and TV stations. I am glad that you took it all onto yourself to establish a local stations' news editorial office and I am writing to suggest a couple of things." And then there are some suggestions. And I'm just going to take it up again at the third page in English, second page in B/C/S. "What is important is that the set of news for the day is formed in one office, editorial office, then faxed (written on the computer in bold capital letters so it is easier to read) and to make sure that the news is broadcast on the local stations frequently. "Miro Toholj probably has a solution for local TV station, and that is sending the tapes through a courier," and so on. Now, this you recognise, don't you, as a communication to Velibor Ostojic, the content of which you are familiar? You're familiar with the content of these communications with Mr. Ostojic at this time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, judging by the style, it could be a letter by Dr. Karadzic sent to Velibor Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Continuing to communicate with you, his former ministers of information, on matters related to controlling the media; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "he," I didn't understand whom you meant, Dr. Karadzic or Velibor Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: The letter's from Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, yes, but he's not sending it to me; he's sending it to Velibor Ostojic, just as he sent the previous one to Vukasinovic. So I did not receive written instructions directly about these things, but even if I had, I don't see the problem. When you are cornered and placed in the situation of an outlaw by the volition of some international representative or a group of people, then you have to respond somehow, to react as individuals, parties react in all such situations. A flow of information has to continue, and I believe there must be international conventions that not only allow it but make it incumbent on us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Could I ask for that document to be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document receives Exhibit Number P6492, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, as forecast, there is just the one matter related to SRT which I wanted to deal with, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter number 25462.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is a report you wrote when you were minister of information. It's a performance report for 1994. I'll read the second and third paragraphs. The third paragraph identifies the TV channel to which we were referring earlier. "Public media's editorial policies (although never clearly defined or strictly regulated), in short, rest on the basic principles of the political and liberation struggle of the Serbian people in former Bosnia-Herzegovina, the creation of Republika Srpska, and its internal development through affirmation of institutions of the system, the Serbian's people aspiration for final state unification, the affirmation of national, historical, and other spiritual values of the Serbian people as a whole. "Apart from around 30 local newspapers and 35 local radio stations, the basic tasks of informing the public was carried out by Serbian Radio and Television Channel One," that's SRT, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: "... SRNA News Agency, the Glas Srpski daily newspaper, the Javnost weekly magazine, and the renewed daily Oslobodjenje." And that's "Srpska Oslobodjenje"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, the Cyrillic version of the "Oslobodjenje."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And just taking it up at the very last page of this report, please. Page 9 of the English, actually, and page 5 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
