utterances.text: It says at the bottom of the page in English, bottom of the page, right, in B/C/S: "The registered media were grouped according to their ownership structure: 17 media were state owned (one television station, two radio stations, 14 magazines and newspapers); two were of mixed ownership (one radio, one magazine); 14 media were privately owned (four radio stations, 10 magazines); four media were owned by civil and legal entities ..." So just to summarise from that, the one television station, SRT, was the state-owned television station; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, its founder was the National Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is your report, you wrote it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I am grateful to you for reminding me of it. I have forgotten these figures, but I see now how democratic we actually were during the war and immediately after it so that the freedom of the media was guaranteed. That was my principle from the very beginning. And I will return to my claim that the ministry was, in fact, the part of the government that provided the logistical support to the media, regardless of whether they were privately owned or state-run or of mixed ownership and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to admit this document, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 1 and 9 in English?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to admit the whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think it would be better to stick with our practice in admitting those put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit the pages shown to the witness, i.e., page 1 and 9 in English. I don't know in B/C/S, but corresponding pages will be admitted as Exhibit P6493.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Just finally to look at SRT briefly. Just remind ourselves, you were on the board for monitoring of programme orientation and editorial policy of the public media, yeah? Yes? It's a decision, I won't bring it up, P01406.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't understand from your question what this refers to.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We'll bring up in that case an earlier version of -- an earlier decision related to this [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 21539. English page 1, B/C/S page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You can see it's the decision very helpfully highlighted as 649.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And we can look at page -- we can look at the -- sorry, second page -- sorry, first page of both.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You can see it's the board for the monitoring of the programme orientation and editorial policy of the public media. Do you understand now what I was asking you about? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's quite clear now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of it. I see that --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And you were a member of that board; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because under Article 2 - and this is a decision of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska - the five members who are representatives of the government and representatives of the media, cultural, and scientific work, consider at that moment I was the editor-in-chief of "Javnost" and that was the logic according to which I became a member of this board, though I wasn't a member of the parliament or a member of the government at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can I admit this -- pages of this decision, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you. SRT --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This receives document number --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- finally --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- P6494, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to look at what SRT, RS state-owned TV, was broadcasting on the 14th of July, 1995, following the fall of Srebrenica. You were minister of information at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's P05236. I apologise, it's the Sanction clip that needs to be played. I should have made that clear.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Enough has been said about the terrorist activities of Srebrenica Muslims in the last few weeks which served as the motive to liberate Srebrenica. But little is known about whom or what the so-called United Nations protected area of Srebrenica has been protecting and hiding. Just in the period between 20th of April and 19th of December, 1992, Srebrenica Muslim terrorists --"

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So that's the start of the broadcast. If we can just move on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The sound quality is terrible. Hardly anything can be heard.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The following Serbian villages were torched: Loznica, Kravica, Podravanje, Hrancici, Brezani, Turija, and Siljkovici. In July, the first villages to perish were Zabokrica and Sandici. On the 3rd of July, Radosevici was destroyed, and Sase on the 4th. Naser Oric's tactics in the summer months were based on launching surprise attacks on the Serbian population working in the fields" --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's enough of this, please. Can we just have the end of the clip. This is 65 ter 40246C.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Dear viewers, the crimes against innocent Serbian civilians committed by Muslims in the past three years in Srebrenica and surrounding areas will be addressed in more detail in a special programme of the Serbian Television which airs immediately after our news. And on this hot day ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It concludes: "... July 14th, the war in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina still goes on with undiminished intensity," and that's from the transcript at 25 -- at 40246C. I didn't want to play all of that footage played on the 14th July on SRT, state-owned TV in Bosnia and Republika Srpska, because it's highly disturbing. You would agree with me, wouldn't you, highly disturbing footage?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, let me tell you that I hope that this is not the report that was cleared from the archives -- the employees of the SRT headed by myself. And secondly, on that day, if it was the 14th of July, I wasn't in Pale. I was abroad, in Rome. I did not watch this. It's the first time that I see the news. There were many horrible instances of footage in videos, both in the media in Sarajevo and in the media in Pale. That was simply the reality. If you did not show what really happened, if you did not show the image of a crime, then the people will not believe you when you tell them anything. That was simply the habit. I myself was not the advocate of such a habit. I know the rules in the West that blood and dead bodies are not to be shown except in Hollywood movies. You do not depict that on the screen; but that was what the editors did. However, while I was the minister for information, you cannot find a single word showing that I called on the editors of the state-run media to some sort of briefing where I would tell them: You will work in this or that way. No, I didn't do it, even though I had a legal right to do that, as those were the professionals who had been quite well-known as journalists even before the war, the well-known people from the joint television in Sarajevo. So it was left to them, to their own conscience and their professional moral and ability to make the TV programmes and also the programmes of the printed press. The ministry did not meddle in that and did not edit the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is what SRT broadcast on the 14th of July, to remind the Serbian population why they should fear and loathe Muslims, just as thousands of Muslim men were being held in schools in Zvornik and executed; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could not be correct because this TV show could have been only be a sort of polemics of low intensity compared with what the TV in Sarajevo and some other TV stations such as Zagreb which could be well received in the Serbian parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, Republika Srpska, if compared to that. There is certainly here what can be called an image as an answer to an image and a word as an answer for a word. So to connect this, if the president did not know this, the president of the country, and if people in the government didn't know, how would these journalists know that something was going on there? After all, they did not visit the fronts. You saw that if that was Srebrenica at all, it was filmed from a distance with a special zoom lens. So your question is not objective.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two things: The transcript and a clarification, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Transcript first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 17 on page 53, it hasn't been recorded something that the witness said: [In English] The report was cleared as you said. As you said. The record that was cleared from the archives as you say. [Interpretation] Lines 18 and 19 on page 53. He did not accept that it was cleared away, but he added "as you say." And another matter is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I -- then for the other matter, I would like you to deal with in your re-examination, which you will start right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you're done --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm done, but can I just tender the last bit of the clip which was 6 --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, I'm grateful, yes. No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives the Exhibit Number P6495, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Toholj.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm for me if you said this "as you say" with regard to the clearing of the archives?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to refer to the recent claim of Madam Prosecutor that the archives, the video archives of the TV have been cleared away, but this document shows that still something has been preserved and has not cleared. So actually, I refuted her claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the question after this insert, it was suggested to you, it was said that it was broadcast with the intention to cause contempt against Muslims. Could you say something about this, whether this piece of news included an invitation for contempt and was something like that broadcast by us?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't an invitation to feel contempt, but we see from the first to the last question, this argument of the OTP that this was terrible propaganda. But the following fact is never taken into account: Namely, that what was broadcast by the other side, from the other side of the demarcation line or separation line, was even more awful and much worse and much more explicit in terms of the contempt that was built into the information and reports and images that were broadcast. Another thing, it is forgotten that I was the one who asked the member of the Presidency, Professor Nikola Koljevic, at one of the meetings held at the airport in Sarajevo, that he should there request under the auspices of the international factor that was present there, to request that the quantity be reduced or that the words be omitted which are insulting on all sides in the media, the phrases rather than claims which would be offensive for the other side and cause anger that was then apparent in the combat operations and just stirred up the war-mongering atmosphere. After that, for a while, we had a sort of media truce for a while so that Professor Koljevic had managed to persuade the other side that they and then us too would exclude the offensive phrases which had been used in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to your knowledge, when did this begin? Did it begin in the war or earlier, this media volleys against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say it in my statement, I gave examples from even 1989. Then in 1990 after the founding of the SDS, the Serbs, especially the leadership of the party and the intellectuals who really had high academic standing, they were academicians, university professors, that was the Political Council that we had, some of them were also members of the party organs, they were called -- they were qualified by words which are improper, that no man should use. Those words were used in the Bosniak media, the media that were under their control. I received one such list of offences in the "As" paper which was unfounded at all, but there were all kinds of qualifications and practically everyone was the target. Some people received even books that were directed against them. You know the book: The death is master, from Serbia, it's a paraphrase of a German writer. Let me not mention the author's name. He used to live in Sarajevo, and he wrote so many heinous texts against all the people he knew that when you even touch the book, you have the impulse to run into the shower and take a shower, have a bath. That was the media atmosphere in which we started our work, focused completely on the wish and the aspiration not to allow chaos to reign. And along those lines, I called on one of the most influential of Izetbegovic's men such as Dzemaludin Latic, I called on him, as he had been in prison with Izetbegovic, to answer the questions of two journalists, one Serb and one Muslim, to publish an interview with him as an editor-in-chief of the Muslim-run "Glas" and one with me as the editor-in-chief of "Javnost." So these were the party publications of the SDS and the SDA, and we should publish it without any redactions for the public and in these two newspapers. So it's an article if anyone wanted to find it - though I think that there is no such wish to establish the exact and actual truth - you would see who advocated what. You would see that the Serbian side speaking through my mouth, if that is the Serbian side, but it is in small part, actually tended to calm down the situation which was already neurotic, and where lives were being lost already. Whereas the other side did not wish to back away from its hard stance. Regardless of the far-reaching consequences, they would not give up the sovereignty by all means, the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina, regardless of the will of one of the constituent peoples in this republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Chamber what this magazine "Voks" was, who was its publisher and how did it treat --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- the peoples in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How does it arise from the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A goodly part of the cross-examination passed in suggestions being made to the effect that Mr. Toholj as the editor-in-chief of "Javnost" and other authors of "Javnost" manipulated the fears felt by the Serbian people, the fears provoked by the events from 1941 to 1945, that they whipped up those fears by manipulating --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But how is that "Voks" related to that? Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I wanted the witness to say because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- it's been shown here what the Serbian side is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and what was that a response to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As you put it, volley is not assisting the Chamber. Shall we continue? Media volley, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My point, Your Excellency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please, please, move on --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- is whether the Serbian side fabricated this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, actually, this is a point that I tried to raise when I objected to the Prosecution about propaganda. If something is propaganda or not depends on what is -- what is true and what is not true. And so if Dr. Karadzic is trying to show that some of the things that are labelled propaganda by the Prosecution and go to the credibility of this witness were, in fact, true, and I think that they've opened the door for him to do that. He's not going to spend -- he could spend years on that but he's only going to do it for a few documents, but he should be allowed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I thought what Mr. Karadzic was going to deal with is the propaganda on the other side. If I was mistaken, I will hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Perhaps also I could assist. The reference was to "Voks" which is a publication, as I understand it, which was a Muslim-published magazine. It's addressed in the witness statement at paragraph 62. I did not cross-examine about this publication. This is not something I cross-examined about, the media volley. I cross-examined about "Javnost" and some other matters, the witness's own denial of crimes. But I didn't cross-examine about this magazine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the very point, Mr. President. The Prosecution opened the subject now to -- he's claiming that -- she's claiming that this witness create -- stoked all of the fears of the Serb community about what could happen, and Dr. Karadzic is trying to show the basis for those fears including --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the witness answered that Muslim side did more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, he did, but some of the specific information that was presented to the public in this publication and perhaps one other document that Dr. Karadzic wants to use, it's only fair that we be allowed to show what that information was. Not only the Prosecution can show that information that this witness was disseminating was designed to be propaganda that promulgated this -- this motive for the Serbs to act. We should show what the actual facts that were shown to the public were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll not allow the question. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then I'm going to start with the latest and then move back towards the beginning. Mr. Toholj, disks were mentioned here that my family sent to Belgrade, to you, and to the committee for truth. Can you tell us, in the briefest possible terms, what kind of material was on these disks and where they ended up, what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were six disks all together. They were Word documents, and it was interviews that you gave to different newspapers that were typed up there. Almost all of that -- well, I cannot remember exactly now whether all of it in its entirety had been published in your book of interviews that Mr. Cavoski and I had edited. So they were published and, therefore, made accessible; but they had been accessible even before that, so we just put it all in one place. So this was a typed-up version in Word in the computer, and we could use that for publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this the only book that the committee published? Or rather, what were all the things that the committee published?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The committee published, in the Serbian and English languages, as its first book your orders that we managed to find. I think that all of your orders are contained there, so as a document, as an original document, as a photograph, if you will. Then we published two books: Your correspondence with statesmen, that is to say, your diplomatic correspondence during the war; and one volume was dedicated to your orders, too, but those that had to do with acts of mercy directed at the enemy. There was an order that we commented upon personally. I objected to you because you allowed an aircraft to fly through, to transport Ismet Bajramovic, Celo, to Italy. I asked you why would he not be treated in Serb hospitals where Muslims and Croats were being treated anyway so then he could be tried later on. So it was everything that the members of the committee for Radovan Karadzic -- that was found was published, and I hope that the OTP and the Chamber and you have copies of these books.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today on pages 7 through 10, what was started on page 98 yesterday continued, namely, this discussion about texts that are warning against dangers from Croatia. And on that page you mentioned the chess-board.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, that is page 96, lines 8 through 24. So the participants can see this and I can also read it out. So 96, page 96, lines 8 through 24, yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what I wanted to ask you. Let us leave aside 1941 to 1945. In 1941, was it necessary to publish these texts concerning current political developments?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. You know that already Franjo Tudjman's book had been published about the minorisation of victims of Jasenovac and other Ustasha camps. This led to rage, fury, reactions among the Serb people no matter where they lived, also among the Jews, too, because truth was being distorted for political reasons. Then some paramilitary units appeared, mainly in the territory of Croatia, and they had old names. I already explained the situation concerning the pits where the remains of innocent civilians were dug up from the Second World War, including members of my own family, and then there were graffiti there: Get these out so that we can throw in new ones. This fear -- well, in military tactics, this -- this is called surprise attacks. So that is the attempt that was made, say, through the front page of "Voks" with your head and Professor Koljevic's head and then when they're playing with my head too as they played that game and so on. Then also impaling the only Nobel prize winner of Yugoslavia, Ivo Andric, so he was impaled on a pen. Very soon after that, one of these unfortunate Bosniaks destroyed his monument on the bridge that he described in his prize-winning novel. So monuments from the Second World War were being destroyed, where the names of our ancestors had been inscribed and they have lost their lives and it doesn't really matter under which flag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure this is assisting the Defence or the Chamber at all. Where are we heading?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, there is a serious accusation levelled here that texts were being published that were warning Serbs of danger, but now I wanted to show what Croatian ministers were doing and writing and what they were preparing. So it's not only paramilitaries. It's two minutes. I wanted to take a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- already ordered on this and the continued questioning and extended answers have the effect of overruling what you've already -- the decision you've made.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at the question of the distinguished Ms. Pack from line 8 onwards and then the answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, then could you explain at what -- to us what you are doing now is not a tu quoque defence, since the Croatian part is doing propaganda, we are doing propaganda as well. Is that your line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Excellency, no. It was being put here that it was unnecessary, superfluous, and even criminal to publish words to the effect that something could happen to the Serbs. I'm trying to show that it wasn't only 1941, but it's also 1991 that was just like 1941. Even a great Jewish writer wrote that 1941 was coming back, Slavko Goldstein. But preparations were being carried out here for attacks against Serbs and killings. Now, were these fears realistic? Was there actually a need to publish this? Or was in just invented for the purposes of false propaganda?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, just a second. It's not relevant, Mr. Karadzic, number one. And number two, it's not a good way to use your time. I'd like to advise to move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Toholj, our letters were referred to here and they were shown, mainly my letters addressed to you and other friends. Can you remember -- actually, first of all, I wanted to ask you when was it that you were no longer director of the television?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was 1998, in March, something like that. I don't remember exactly. In my CV you can find the date for how long I was director. It was only four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember in those letters what was it that I knew about what happened in Srebrenica? And what were my convictions about that? Later on, up until that moment, what was it that I had found out about what had happened in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I remember. In one letter you had received some --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- information that in Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness can't answer the question: What was it that I found out about what had happened in Srebrenica? He can't answer the question what Dr. Karadzic knew. I don't know if this is a reference to the letter that I took the witness to, but this particular question can't be answered by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it Mr. Karadzic was asking what he came to know through their communications, but probably Mr. Karadzic can reformulate his question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was hoping that I was clear, but I wasn't maybe. This was my question: [In English] Do you remember in those letters what was it that I knew about what happened in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How could he know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that's the same question, really, Dr. Karadzic. What this witness can deal with are those matters which he personally told you about or was present when somebody else told you about. Other than that, he'd be second-guessing what was in your mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I'm probably not being clear. I'm asking whether the witness remembers what it was that I wrote to him at that moment about what I knew. What kind of knowledge I presented in my letters sent to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that would be encompassed in what I said. That would be a communication between you two.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we take a look at 1D49022.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this letter and was it published in your book?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the letter. It was published in my book -- in our book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 10 in e-court in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please do focus on this paragraph now that starts with the words: "I have assurances ..." What was it that I presented to you about my own knowledge at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is written here is that you have received information that some Serb mercenaries - I don't know exactly by name who this refers to, I personally do not know - really killed people after the fall of Srebrenica not in that location itself. They did it on orders from the French and that this is reliable information. That is what you are writing. It is interesting that the Muslim authorities are not commenting upon this, although this was published and this is very accusatory. I remember that it was during the telecast of the trial of Drazen Erdemovic, a Croat who had surrendered, and you heard a sentence of his uttered before this Court, Erdemovic: "'We received a ... strict order from higher levels of command to take care of civilians and prisoners of war, but my platoon commander did not respect that.' His platoon commander was this Pelemis who was arrested together with the group called 'Spider,'" Pauk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you believe that, that that is what I knew in the year 2000, Mr. Toholj? Did you believe that? Did you believe that I was addressing you in all sincerity? I'll rephrase. How does this fit into your knowledge about my position and my knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in view of the number of dilemmas regarding what happened in Srebrenica and around Srebrenica, this left an impression on me that you finally got some knowledge that we could hang on to in terms of what had actually happened there, so that we fill this void in terms of what it was that had actually happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this letter be admitted and these two pages, whatever you wish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I don't know what the rest of the letter says and how long the rest of the letter is. I'd prefer to be able to see the -- the entire of the letter rather than just this extract.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless you have an objection otherwise, we'll admit this portion following our practice. We'll give the next Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit Number D3992, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before I put my last question, Your Honours, paragraph 14 of my indictment refers to what I wanted to clarify a moment ago regarding my role in the propaganda. I don't know how to defend myself from this paragraph, 14, especially item (C) in paragraph 14. I'm not allowed to present my defence on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Karadzic, that's not a fair statement. The Chamber never prohibited you from defending yourself from -- against the allegation in the indictment. Never.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say you prohibited me. I said I'm disabled from defending myself. My assertion was that the information was not propaganda, that was not false information, but if the Croatian minister of defence says that they should be called upon in their homes and shot in the stomach and there were arms shipments through Hungary, then it's not false information to warn of the danger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Discuss with your legal advisers how to proceed and how to defend with respect to those allegations in the indictment, and shall we continue now. You said you have your final question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Toholj, the Prosecution has tried to prove something that you probably don't even dispute, namely, two things: One, that you hold me in high esteem, which is probably mutual; and that we were close. Now I want to ask you: Do you hold me in high esteem because we are close or are we close because you have respect for me?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is the latter. You are older than I am, one generation ahead of me, especially as an author, but from the moment I met you we were friends because I first had great respect for you as a poet and an author and later as a politician. While I worked at the secretary of the association of writers, you will remember that your ideas were welcomed there. You were against the politicisation of such an organisation, you were a physician specialising in a very delicate branch of medicine, and you were held in great respect even in barrooms, in every company. I have always held you in high esteem as a person and as an author, as all these other things you are. I don't believe in the allegations that are in your indictment. We were not always physically close. We were sometimes at very great distances, but I don't believe in all these allegations in the indictment that want to portray us as the guilty party, but I will leave it to the Chamber to make its own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me if you remember whether ethnic nationalist themes were frequent in our discussions and what did I think about your ethnic affiliation after we got to know each other better and started to respect each other?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out from a friend that, at some point long after we got to know each other, you initially thought, judging by my name, that I am of a different ethnicity, a Croat or Catholic or something, but you didn't mind because I know you have many friends in Catholic monasteries in Presevo and in Fojnica. I know that because when I needed some spiritual shelter, I would briefly go to those monasteries to take a rest and had many friends there. Before the SDS party you established another party which was the Greens in Sarajevo. So you didn't have that problem with peoples of other races, ethnicities, nations. And it's obvious from the books that I published, although some people say those books should never have been published, I believed it was a step towards liberating the truth, a struggle which was very rarely successful in our parts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 16, what is missing is that I formed the Greens party together with a Muslim woman, a Bosniak woman. That bit is missing from the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since I heard that everything about a personality matters before a Tribunal such as this, I wanted to also ask you about the literary awards I received, et cetera, but I won't go into that. Thank you very much for your collaboration and for your friendship, but I'm glad to say that respect comes before friendship still. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless my colleagues have a question for you, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Toholj. Thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You're free to go. We'll rise all together. We'll have a break for 45 minutes. And next witness is, I take it, Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume at quarter past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.28 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Popovic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Could the counsel assisting Mr. Popovic introduce himself for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Zoran Zivanovic. I am counsel for Mr. Vujadin Popovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Popovic, do you need anything? Do you have a problem with --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was receiving interpretation into another language but it's all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you understand the proceeding in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you are well aware of this, but before you commence your evidence I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at this International Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood, Your Honour, but I believe that will not occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Popovic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was very quick. We need to make a short pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, can you tell us whether you have given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up in e-court 1D09190. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see that statement on the screen, the front page?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read and signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the last page, please, for the witness to identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you have stated to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, that's it, with perhaps minor clarifications that I will need to add probably during examination viva voce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is anything incorrect or inaccurate in this statement, anything wrong?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions today, would your answers be essentially the same, not verbatim but essentially the same?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Objection at this point, Your Honour. I think the witness is trying to leave some wiggle room, speaking about perhaps minor clarifications, I don't think so, if there is anything incorrect. I'd like the -- it to be put to the witness: Is the statement correct or not. And if he's got any clarifications to make them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's fair enough. If you could deal with it, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, is this statement accurate and is there any need for you to make any corrections or changes?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: The statement is accurate and there is no need for me to change or correct it. That is not what I meant earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document receives Exhibit Number D3993, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out in English a short summary of Colonel Vujadin Popovic's statement. [In English] Vujadin Popovic was chief of security of the Drina Corps during July 1995. At that time he held the rank of lieutenant-colonel. At that time, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic arrived in Srebrenica on July the 11th, 1995, after the Bosnian Serb Army had entered the town. On the morning of 12th of July, 1995, he was at the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac for a meeting convened by General Mladic. He knew of no plan to execute men from Srebrenica at that time and emphatically denies the claim by Prosecution Witness Momir Nikolic that he stated that the men were to be killed during a conversation on the morning of 12th of July outside the Hotel Fontana. On 13th of July, 1995, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic travelled along the road from Bratunac to Nova Kasaba. He saw between 100 and 200 prisoners standing or sitting by the road near Sandici. He did not see anyone being killed or mistreated. Later, in the afternoon, he saw about 800 prisoners on the football-pitch in Nova Kasaba and observed a soldier making a list of the prisoners. When he passed the warehouse in Kravica that evening, he saw bodies on the ground. When he inquired what had happened, the policemen at the warehouse told him that there had been an incident and refused to be more specific. In the morning of 14th of July, 1995, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic participated in the transport of a convoy of vehicles carrying prisoners from Bratunac to Zvornik. He understood that the prisoners were to be housed temporarily in school buildings in the Zvornik area. During 14th of July, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic observed prisoners being held at schools in Orahovac and Rocevic. During his stay in Orahovac and Rocevic, he did not see any killing of prisoners of war. At that time, he was not aware that there was any plan for the prisoners to be executed. Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic learned on 15th of July that prisoners had been executed at Orahovac, Petkovci, and Rocevic the day before. On 16th of July, while in Pilica, he learned that other prisoners had been executed at the cultural centre there. He told his commander, General Krstic, about these killings when he saw him in person on 18th of July, 1995. On 23rd of July, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic was in the Bisina area where he saw the bodies of about 30 prisoners who appeared to have been executed by soldiers. He was shaken by what he saw and ordered the men to bury the bodies. Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic never informed President Karadzic about the execution of prisoners from Srebrenica. He is not aware of the existence of any written reports which contained information about the executions. He never heard anyone suggest that President Karadzic was informed about the execution of prisoners or that he had approved it. Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic was convicted of his role in the Srebrenica events by this Tribunal and sentenced to life imprisonment in the first degree. His case is currently on appeal. And that would be a short summary. Now I would like to present to Colonel Popovic two of his own documents from this time and pose some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to note, line 19, page 76, line 19-20, the statement does not say where he saw the bodies of about 30 prisoners who appear to have been executed by soldiers. It says he saw 30 bodies there. There is nothing about appearing to have been executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That may be inquired of the witness by Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we'll leave that for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like Mr. Karadzic to clarify because he said that they appeared to have been executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it -- sorry, if I could just respond, if he says something is in the statement when it's not in the statement, that's not a matter for my cross-examination; that's a matter for reading a correct summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's possible, Your Excellencies, and Mr. Nicholls, that as the summary is not evidence, I was perhaps a bit too flexible when re-telling the statement. It's not evidence; it's my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, from your official position, could you observe what was going on in Srebrenica at the beginning of this combat action of separating the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the combat action of separating the enclaves, I was in Vlasenica at my command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And could you notice -- were you in the field on the 7th or did you receive a report from the field or did you have your men in the field who would report to you about what was going on?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with the principle of organisation of security service in the Army of Republika Srpska, each unit of the size of brigade had a security organ or intelligence and security organ within its composition, depending on the title of the unit. So I did have such men who sent such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up in e-court 65 ter 02074.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for this to appear on the screen, Colonel, could you tell us what an organ denotes when we say "an organ," and is there also something else apart from an organ?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with the organisation, as I said, the security organ is lower than, for example, a security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember this document which you forwarded after your organ reported this to you, and could you tell us, what did you think of this line that the civilians from Srebrenica are moving -- are being moved towards Zepa as early as the 7th of July?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Just, please, let me read all of it and then I will give you my answer. I simply have nothing to say here, no comment is needed. The issue was that the civilian population was slowly moving out from these border areas where combat operations were ongoing and they were moving inside. So the preparation of the population for evacuation had been carried out earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives the Exhibit Number D3994, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just, just -- just to clarify, what -- first of all, I'm a bit behind because there was no proofing note about these two documents which were added. I'm not objecting to them on that basis, but I asked Mr. Robinson about this before court and he didn't know, but they had been discussed in proofing but we received nothing. Which enclave are we talking about? Because it says here: "The observed activities indicate that the enemy is evacuating small groups of civilians from the Zepa enclave ..." That's what we're talking about, not Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we can ask the witness. Something is wrong about the translation. I just -- I was just informed about this. "According to the report of the organ towards Srebrenica" and it's translated "from, towards Zepa" instead of "from Zepa."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, can you please read out for us this sentence so that it can be translated.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: "The observed activities indicate that the enemy is evacuating small groups of civilians towards the Zepa enclave along the Petrovica Brdo-Caurka-Pribojevici-Grebici village axis in front of the forward lines in the brigade's area of defence."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope it's been clarified now. I think the problem is in the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware, were you informed about where our army was, where the UNPROFOR units were, that is to say, their check-points, and how did you obtain such information? Or, more specifically, was UNPROFOR always at the location that was agreed on so that you would know judging by a map where they were located?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: We had in maps and that was also the part of the agreement drawn locations where UNPROFOR was supposed to be. However, that did not correspond to the actual situation on the ground. They moved their check-points because of their own needs, sometimes because they needed to organise communications and sometimes because at certain points in time the Muslim forces -- or rather, in certain places, locations, they would take control of those locations. So they had to move their check-points into the depth of our territory. Of course we knew where the check-points were. This is rather something that has to do with the area towards Zepa. I think it's coming from Mr. Kaldesic who was the security organ in the Milici Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have a look at 1D9192.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, could you please tell us whether for our forces it was important to know whether they had moved or not? Why was it important to know where they were --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Objection, leading --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- if not in the location where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Objection, leading, "why was it important for us to know"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it important that the Army of Republika Srpska should exactly know where they were and why?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Of course it was important, the exact locations where they were, where the observation post was, where they patrolled, because it would happen, as you know, that someone would pass through their lines and fire at our side and our units returned fire. At that moment, they could be the target of the fire if they were not in the agreed location. It was also because of the agreement to separate the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please present this document to us. It is on the following day with regard to the previous one. Who is writing this and what is requested here? And to whom is it addressed?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's clear from this telegram what is requested. The information is requested - it is to be sent to the Drina Corps command - as to whether the check-point in Biljeg is still under our control and which of the other UNPROFOR check-points are under our control and whether they are threatened by our units. It's very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe, I'm not sure, that the translation is wrong, that is to say, "threatened by our units," I would say or "are in jeopardy from our units," but I'm not sure. I'm not sure about this translation, whether they are really threatened by our units or -- it's better for you to read it. Under our control. You can read it and we can ask the interpreters to literally interpret it. Which from here and which others.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: It says clearly here: "Inform us urgently whether the UNPROFOR check-point in Biljeg is still under our control there, which other UNPROFOR check-points are under our control or if they are threatened by our units, or if they are threatened by our units. "And likewise, urgently tell us what lines were reached along the axis of our unit's attack." That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are requesting this from Kosoric; correct?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why did you request this?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Probably there were objections from UNPROFOR lodged with commander of our unit and he requested immediately for the information, to check whether this was true or not and what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And for what purpose? To what end?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: In order to avoid that the UNPROFOR units be targeted by the fire coming from our units, so that's the only thing that can follow from this telegram, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I stick to my objection that "threatened" is wrong and that it should be that they are in jeopardy because a threat --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- is a wilful activity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do not waste your time. If you have some problem with the translation, please -- there are ways to do it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. Can this document be admitted, please? And at this moment I have no more questions for Colonel Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number D3994 -- 95, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, are you satisfied with Mr. Karadzic's clarification as to the bodies in Bisina?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, he said he was editorialising, if I understood him, and that was his view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're serving a life sentence, right, right now?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Highest sentence that can be passed by this Tribunal; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: That's also true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. And this honourable Court here in this Tribunal, in this building, actually many times in this room, sat through 425 trial days before they found you guilty beyond reasonable doubt; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was pronounced guilty beyond reasonable doubt, but I appealed against it because I have some objections to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've answered the question --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: -- and I think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one clarification. Not this room. Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Courtroom III, yes, Your Honour. Sometimes in here, but you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Found guilty of persecutions, correct, for murder and inhumane treatment?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Found guilty of murder; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: That's what the judgement says or how it reads, but I have objections to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, I didn't ask you if you had objections. Right now I'm just confirming with you that you know what you've been convicted of and to make it clear to everybody who is with us today. You've been found guilty of extermination, mass murder; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: But just with regard to your previous sentence let me say that this should mean in advance that something is wrong, about the fact that I've been sentenced or convicted for this. And then it's listed there under specific items. You know quite well because you participated in our proceedings, you know what I have been convicted for and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, I realise that you've appealed. That's beside the point at the moment. You were also found guilty of genocide; correct?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the Trial Chamber, in finding you guilty of these crimes, in paragraph 1179 of the judgement, found that you were not a marginal participant in the JCE to murder. "The evidence shows that he," you, "was entrenched in several aspects of the operation and that he participated with resolve." And then in the next paragraph they stated: "... the scale of the atrocities committed to his knowledge, his vigorous participation in several aspects of the massive killing operation, in particular his direct participation in the organisation of large-scale murders at Grbavci School (where between 800 and 2500 Bosnian Muslims were killed), Rocevic School (where approximately 1.000 Bosnian Muslims were killed), and Pilica (where between 1.000 and 2.000 Bosnian Muslims were killed)." That's what -- the way the Trial Chamber characterised your participation; you know that, right, that you vigorously participated in this massive killing operation?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I hope that through this testimony we'll get a clearer picture of all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. You hope to help your appeal by testifying here today; that's why you're coming to testify before your appeal is heard. Is that right? Is that what you just said?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. In my appeal, I presented everything where I believe I was damaged and where I believe that the Trial Chamber did not pay enough attention to Defence witnesses and other testimonies, but rather than that a priori the Prosecution witnesses who were not quite telling the truth were those who were taken into account and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: -- that mostly made me --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand -- I understand. Now, it's not just you who's been convicted in the security branch for these murders, these mass murders in July 1995. Your superior in the professional chain, Beara, Beara, also convicted of genocide in the same trial as you; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, but what does it have to do with -- I mean, Beara and me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me for laughing. The security officer below you in the Zvornik Brigade, Drago Nikolic, also convicted aiding and abetting genocide; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Tolimir, above Beara, also convicted of genocide; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I did not follow Tolimir's trial. I don't know what was dealt with there, but I know that he has been convicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you know that Trbic, Drago Nikolic's subordinate was convicted of genocide in the State Court? So from Main Staff down to brigade. Do you know that Trbic was convicted?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And of course, your commander, Krstic, was convicted of genocide and then aiding and abetting genocide; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. 12 July, we'll go through some of these places. I read out a paragraph to you about the Trial Chamber talking about your vigorous participation at Grbavci school, Orahovac, Rocevic, and Pilica, where your statement says you were at different times. But first let's go to Potocari, 12 July. And in your statement it's clear you were in Potocari on 12 July and you're on video there; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, and you went there with General Mladic after the Hotel Fontana meeting that day; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When did you go?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: After the meeting ended, the one at the Fontana Hotel, I set off for the Bratunac Brigade. In front of the Bratunac Brigade, General Mladic met me and ordered me - it was just like this - to take this truck with bread and a tank truck and drive it up there, distribute it up there to the men -- --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: -- to the people who gathered --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, sorry. Sorry, I'm not trying to cut you off, but that's not my point. My point is that - and I see what you're saying - after the Hotel Fontana meeting at the Bratunac Brigade, General Mladic ordered you to go to Potocari and then you went to Potocari; right? I'm just trying to get the time and sequence?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And while you were there, you were there, this is your statement at paragraph 24, you were there for about two hours; right? That's what you say?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you got some documents from the police station and then went back to the brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: That was on the 11th when I took the documents from the Srebrenica MUP and brought that to the brigade. When we were in Srebrenica, and that's also recorded. I'm passing by and Mladic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: -- tells me: Take this computer, and only the keyboard and the monitor were actually left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So then you returned to the Bratunac Brigade and then you start going through and examining those documents you got from Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: What date was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 12th, 12th.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: So on the 12th after the -- after an unpleasant scene with General Mladic when, because of juice or beer, whatever it was to be distributed, when he tried to kick me, I was a bit ashamed in front of all these people who were there --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to object as non-responsive --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I just went away and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me read your statement to you, you can look at yours, paragraph 24 and 25. "I estimate that I spent one or two hours in Potocari that day," this is after Mladic kicks you. "While I was there, Muslim men were not segregated out nor did I see any crime." Paragraph 25: "I returned to the Bratunac Brigade command, went to the office allocated to me, and began to sort and examine documents I'd collected at the Srebrenica MUP." That's correct; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you don't go back to Potocari that day, on the 12th, after you get back to the brigade?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You don't go anywhere? You just finish working on your documents until 6.00 when you go out to dinner?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I got there around -- after 2.00, and then I threw everything onto the floor from these two sacks and began sorting it out in accordance with my opinion what was more urgent to review because it was dusty and everything, so I wanted to arrange everything. It lasted for perhaps an hour and a half. After that, I went outside and I met my classmate Savo Cvetinovic, who I hadn't seen since my time in Drvar -- or rather, Bihac, I apologise. That was the last time we saw each other so we said: Okay, let's go to my place. Someone was there, whether it was my sister or someone, and we went to his place to have dinner together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And your statement says at about 1800 hours Savo Cvjetinovic came by the brigade and then that's when you go out to have dinner; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, could I have P04388, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is your report from 12 July, your activities that day. It's at 1730 hours from the DK forward command post Bratunac, strictly confidential number 08-446-6 [sic], to the Main Staff, sector for intelligence and security, and also to the security command at the Drina Corps. I know you're very familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, so we need to go over in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "A refugee group of about 30- to 35.000 women and children, elderly ..." et cetera, you're discussing the situation there with the women and children, old people and sick. Then you say: "About 5.000 women and children were evacuated so far. We are separating men from 17 - 60 years of age and we are not transporting them. We have about 70 of them so far and the security organs and the DB /state security/ are working with them." And let's go back to the first paragraph. "In the course of the day, our forces and MUP forces did not have any heavy exchange of fire with balijas ..." This is you reporting on your report separating men, people you refer to as balijas, and not transporting them; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, how can I report on something that I did not do? Take a look at the document. I have to explain this document. Look. I mean, your statement, your claim, is wrong. The document is typical for the reporting of subordinate organs to superior organs. The enemy, our forces, UNPROFOR, et cetera. Secondly, look at the number in the heading. It is not my number at all. My number was 17 as far as I know. Thirdly, why am I sending a document to myself? I'm sending myself a document, I mean there is no point. Until this document was shown to me after our trial, I did not know of the existence of this document and that's why we asked to have it admitted. I'm expressing a serious doubt that I personally wrote that. After all, your witness said that to you, I did not take part in the separation or any activity that has to do with this in Potocari. And all of that has been proven.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's -- your guilt has been proven. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I would ask that Mr. Nicholls not make any comments. Dr. Karadzic was criticised for that by Mr. Nicholls and others, and so they shouldn't now be allowed to do something they know is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's not a comment. It's a question to the witness. He's now saying that our witnesses showed he had nothing to do with Potocari; that is not correct. That is not the truth of the evidence in his trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you done or do you have more on this document?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would like to make a digression in relation to your assertion. I remember how many witnesses went through our trial. Not a single witness mentioned that Popovic did anything in Potocari, did not separate, did not do anything. And now you are stating to me: "Your guilt has been proven." What does that have -- what does this relate to? This or something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. You just testified here under oath that you didn't see this document until after your trial, and I think you just might have messed up in your story. Look at paragraph 27 of your statement, look at paragraph 27 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have your statement, Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I beg your pardon. I have it, yes. I spoke in haste. Actually --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Wait, wait, wait, wait -- no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I saw him --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Wait for my question. I haven't asked a question yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want this turn into a quarrel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, there was a question pending and Mr. Nicholls is obligated to let the witness answer the question before he puts his next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There wasn't a question pending other than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- because of the -- due to the lack of interpretation, we didn't hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So after you said: "Actually," we didn't hear anything, could you repeat what you said, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what that relates to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then I will ask Mr. Nicholls to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll just make the question very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All I'd asked you to do was to look at paragraph 27 of your statement. You just testified you never saw this document until after your trial. In paragraph 27, the last sentence, which is all about this document, says: "I read this telegram at the Drina Corps command the next day, 13 July 1995." So when you wrote your statement you thought that was the best option to deal with this document. Where you're sitting here today, you forgot you said that and thought it was better to say you hadn't seen it until after trial; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Nicholls. No, not at all. Quite simply, I said -- sorry, I got carried away because you irritated me with this question before that and I got a bit lost. So it is correct, the next day, because I told this one -- I mean, why would I be sending myself a document? It is correct the next day when I came up there I read this document. Once again, I apologise. Quite simply, I got lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you also just told me and established that you were at the Bratunac Brigade command after you got back to Potocari and that you stayed there sorting through documents until you left to have dinner with your old friend Savo at 1800, 6.00 p.m. This document, by your own testimony, goes out at 5.30 when you're at the Bratunac Brigade and it goes out from Bratunac. So is your testimony that while you were at the Bratunac Brigade, without talking to you, somebody else, without your knowledge, sends out a report from the Drina Corps security officer's name while he's in the building without telling him?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, that building is not one room where everybody is sitting. There are certain offices there. I was in an office.
