When I arrived, Momir Nikolic gave me the keys to that office because I guess that man was absent. I moved into that office. I closed the door. I got this material out and started sorting it. I don't know who was at the command at that moment, whether somebody was there, whether somebody was walking around. I wasn't interested at all. I was doing my work which I thought was urgent, to see what all of this was about, these documents that I had seized and brought from Srebrenica from the MUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. Again, so your story --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We could not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise. I thought you were done. Do you have anything else to add?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So that means your story is you're sitting in an office, with papers spread out all around you on the floor, doing your security tasks, and somebody in the building - in your statement you say you think it's Momir Nikolic - without your knowledge sends out a report under your name without telling you. They're trying to frame you, thinking there might be a trial in 2008?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Very pretentious. That's not what I meant. That's not what I thought. Quite simply, I was working on the job that I thought should have been done, and who got there probably thought that I was there and signed for me. But I would like to see the original, to see whose signature is there, because only the name and surname remain once it is sent for encoding. However, without a signature it cannot be sent out for encryption. Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I don't think we need to go over it much, but when -- in the VRS when somebody signs for, "za," a commander or an assistant commander for security, like yourself, that means they've approved it; right? It means the person whose name is on it has approved it?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily approved. Perhaps the person is simply not there at that moment and this other person just signs this "za" and sends it on. I know that from experience when I worked at the command. If the commander is not there for the moment, then the Chief of Staff signs for him and the document is sent with the commander's signature, and the commander himself may be absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But what you've just testified to under oath is that you were there, so it wouldn't -- you weren't absent, so it wouldn't have gone out under your name without your consent, without your approval?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, this is the fifth time I'm saying this -- I don't know which time. I was not consulted about that. I was in the office where the door was closed, and whether somebody knew I was there or not -- maybe they thought I was not in the building. How would they know that Popovic was there? It's not that Popovic stuck a badge there as he entered saying: Popovic is in such and such an office. You know, I don't know whether he knew that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Testimony in this case, your honest, truthful testimony is that you can be in the Bratunac Brigade without Momir Nikolic, the Bratunac Brigade security officer, knowing that his Drina Corps superior is there when you're working there for hours?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely. Momir Nikolic was doing certain things in Potocari and he himself says in his statement that we did not meet up there, so how could he know where I was moving about? And why would I have to tell him: Listen, Momir, I'm going here and there? It is he who is supposed to report to me, not I that am supposed to report to him. That is how things work in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this document -- our position is that you wrote it and it came from you and it described what you were doing. That's our position. Describes the Muslims, uses the term "balijas," and that's a term you used for Muslims, isn't it? That's found in paragraph 1193 of your trial judgement?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Please show me another document where this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. We'll take a moment. We'll get to that. Okay, so are you denying you used the term "balijas"? You never used the term "balijas," is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say before I see this other document too --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, just a second --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: -- I mean as far as I can remember, as far as I can remember, to the best of my recollection, it's been a long time after all. I cannot be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So until you see a document that proves it, you can't be sure whether you used the term "balijas," is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: How can I after all these years, this kind of expression? I don't know whether you can assume what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can I have P04390, please. I'm sorry that's not clearer. If we could blow up the top corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is from -- this is a document that goes out on the 18th of July from Momir Nikolic. It's got an 08 number on the top, which is the reason why you said with the document that goes out under your name you thought it was from Momir Nikolic, that's in your statement. And this goes out under Momir Nikolic's name if we look at the bottom. Don't worry about the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now could we go to the next page in the Serbian and the English. Next page in Serbian, additional page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the handwritten version there - and this has been explained in this trial - I'll make it very short terms -- very short, was written by Colonel Jankovic. That's the handwritten document, report. And Mr. Nikolic explained in his testimony here on 14 of February, 2012, at T 24682 to 24683, the way this document was created, which was that he was working with Colonel Jankovic in the Bratunac Brigade. Colonel Jankovic wrote out this document for him, put his initials on the bottom - if you go to the bottom of the handwritten version -- or we have to go to the next page, I guess, again - and then Momir Nikolic took it to be transmitted. And after it was transmitted, both versions came back. So when Momir Nikolic sends something out under somebody else's name, because they've told him to do it and he's at his brigade, it just goes out under his name, which is why your order that you sent went out under your name; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. These are two different documents, two different things. Probably Momir Nikolic was present while this man was writing this. I mean, you cannot just compare things that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And your document - we don't need to bring it back up - you kept saying: Why would I send it to myself? Why would I send it to myself? Well, first of all, it's sent to the Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: It was sent to the Main Staff and the Drina Corps and the security organ. To myself, I should not be sending things to myself. I had the version -- I should have a version that is supposed to be encoded. Why would I be sending this to myself? I mean, then I could just send it to the Main Staff, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Because you send it to the Main Staff and because you're at the Bratunac Brigade, you send it to yourself so that at the Drina Corps you'd have a record right there at the Drina Corps in the security branch of what was sent that day about you separating balijas.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying to you yet again, I get the document back from the encryption people, that is to say, once they type it up, they return the document to me. And I don't need a new document over there. I take that document. And when I go up there, I put it in my archives. And secondly, I repeat yet again, I did not send it. You keep insisting that I sent it. I did not send it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 65 ter 04398, please. This wasn't on my list; it's just come up, the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll try to make this very quick. Drina Corps -- this is, as it's coming up, a Drina Corps command security department, 29 April 1995, from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we go to the next page of the English, it's page 2 of the English, please. The Serbian's fine where we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The last sentence from you: "All VRS members are to be informed through appropriate command organs about the information that balijas are liquidating Serbs in Switzerland," whatever that means. So you use the term "balijas" in this document; does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just read the entire document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Actually, I missed one. Sorry. Go to page 1 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You can keep reading in your version. You use it twice here. It's in the first sentence under 2: "Security organs of the Drina Corps received an information that a balija, by the name of" so and so. So you use the word "balija" twice in this document.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is correct that the word "balija" was used twice. But what is interesting to me is the first line, where it says the security organs of the Drina Corps received information, that is to say that I received that information. And probably -- well, maybe, maybe, that's what it said in those documents, balija Omerovic, and then it was just copied that way. But I should warn you about what this word means. I mean, the word "Chetnik" was used here --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If -- if -- if --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's a derogatory term too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I know that. If I want your explanation of what the word means, I'll ask you to explain it. Okay? I'm just asking if you used it because supposedly you couldn't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 65 ter 04397, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is from 20 September 1995. The first one was before Srebrenica and this one is after.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Go to the second page so Mr. Popovic can see who sent this. Of the Serbian, please. Okay. This one is signed -- can we go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I really want to make this quick, Mr. Popovic. I'm just trying to confirm that you used these terms since you've contested it or can't remember. In the English, in the first full paragraph, and this isn't forwarding information it doesn't look like: "Lately in pre-trial proceedings against balijas captured in the former Zepa enclave ..." there is a danger here about documenting crimes apparently. And paragraph 4, if we could go to that in the English, next page, and you can see it in your version. "A special problem so far has been the case when a captured balija (from whichever unit of the ABiH) after being registered by the Red Cross or any other international humanitarian organisation, escapes or is killed while attempting escape ..." So the only question I'm asking you is: Do you recall now that you used the term "balijas," same term we see in that 12 July report?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is evident, it seems, that sometimes - very rarely - I used it, but that doesn't mean that I used it on the 12th of July. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. In the afternoon of 13 July now, okay, moving ahead to 13 July -- could you please close your statement. You know, if you need to look at it, just ask and we'll let you look at it, but just close it for now. Okay? Thanks. That way we can tell what you're remembering as opposed to what you're reading. In the afternoon at Nova Kasaba -- in the afternoon of 13 July at some point you were in Nova Kasaba and you see a field with about 800 prisoners on it; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember running into Zvonko Bajagic, Duga Puska there?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: That -- I think they called him Duga Puska, but I don't remember that, but I know that I was there, that I stopped the car, parked near the end of the football-pitch. I talked to Malinic -- actually, I saw Malinic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, okay --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: -- I don't remember seeing Zvonko. It's probably this void in my memory, but I just don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, maybe this will help you remember. He testified in this case that he was there and that he met you. That's at T 41149 in this trial, 10 July this year. And his testimony is that you prevented pictures being taken of those captured Muslims and that one way or another you took the camera and exposed the film to the light because one of the people with Zvonko Bajagic was taking pictures of these Muslims and you stopped that, you destroyed the film. Do you remember that? Another void?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, do I remember it? I don't, but if I did that and if he says that I did that, then maybe it is the truth. But I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know at what time. Give me some guide-line. I was there in the morning -- actually, in all fairness there weren't any prisoners there then. I left the APC there and then went to Vlasenica and then perhaps in the afternoon/early evening when I was going back from Vlasenica --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You say, it's in your -- you say it's when you saw Zoran Malinic there with 800 prisoners, Zvonko Bajagic says it's in the afternoon. I'm not concerned about the exact time, I don't see what that has to do with it, it's when you're there when you see the field full of prisoners. Now, why would you destroy that film? You said "maybe I did."

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that already then Mladic had ordered that prisoners -- I mean that prisoners be moved from those places or Gvero's order to provide security for them better and then that no filming be allowed. Perhaps that would be the only explanation. I don't remember that particular act at all. Talking to the soldiers there, I remember that. I remember Mladic coming. This I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me suggest another explanation. You said that was the only possible explanation. Think about this possible explanation: That you knew all those men were going to be killed and you didn't want photos of them floating around, so you destroyed the evidence that any of those men who happened to be photographed were alive at that field?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what would I know that at that moment? How can you take things so out of context, you knew at that point in time? You're following my movement on the 12th, you're following my movement on the 13th. How could I know that at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you've been found to have known that. I'm surprised you don't have any clue of how you could know that. I'll tell you how you could know that because you were part of the murder operation on that day, and what you were doing on that day was working to make sure that every captured Muslim male was murdered; that's how you would know it.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: On that day there were no killings, that's one. And two, how was I participating in killings when I came there by APC and then went to Vlasenica? Where did I participate on that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is your truthful testimony here that on 13 July 1995, after the fall of Srebrenica, there were no killing of prisoners? Is that what you just said? And do you mean that?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Not that I know, not that I know of. I'm saying this emphatically under oath, not that I know of. As far as I know, that day there were none, no killings that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, we're going to move on, on that day. And that same day, 13 July, going back to Bratunac, this is paragraph 36 of your statement, you don't need to read it unless you need to remember. I'm just telling the Trial Chamber where to find it. You stopped by the Kravica warehouse where you see several dozen bodies on the ground in front of the hangar. That's another execution site that you happened to be at during this time, right, in addition to Pilica and the other ones we'll get to?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I was not there at the time of the killing. I was returning that evening, stopped by and saw those people executed. I asked what happened. They told me there was an incident. Those were not executions that I was present at. Please don't put to me things that are not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My point is you just said at page 105, speaking about the 13th: "As far as I know, that day there were none, no killings that I know of." Now, same day, 13 July, according to your own statement, you were at Kravica warehouse with a bunch of bodies, dead bodies, out front. Are you now claiming those bodies were not victims of killings? That's the only way your story is even halfway coherent.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not claiming those were not the bodies of victims. Those were the men that were killed in that incident and I saw them when I was passing by, but I thought you were saying that at the pitch, when I was passing by near Kasaba, I knew that executions had taken place. That's what I thought you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. But what -- understand my point is you said after that to the best of your knowledge there were no executions on the 13th, and that's not true. There were executions on the 13th, right, at Kravica? Forget about Sandici and Jadar. At Kravica you know there were executions on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat, as I was passing by, I saw the bodies, I stopped, asked: What happened? They told me: There has been an incident. That's all I knew at that time. In my earlier answer I meant the other thing by the football field and that's why this came out. Mistakes happen because you put things out of context --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: -- I mean, you're practically asking me to make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just go over this Kravica situation which we did not have during your trial. A witness who was just here, Tomo Kovac, spent about 50 per cent of his time answering questions saying that the MUP in this area were resubordinated to the army. You are the Drina Corps chief of security. You're at the warehouse. You ask the policemen there what happened, resubordinated policemen. They wave their hands at you: No, we don't want to talk about it, and you accept that. There's nothing the chief of security of the Drina Corps can do to find out what happened when he's standing in front of a warehouse with bodies lying all around him?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My question is: Why do you accept, if we believe your story, that these policemen waved their hands at you and that's why you don't find out anything about this "incident"? Why didn't you say: Hey, I'm commander -- assistant commander for security of the Drina Corps, tell me what happened here to those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I will answer this question now. First of all, you said a moment ago that I was at the warehouse. I was not at the warehouse; I was on the road, on the road, standing by my car. Second, every soldier of the police who was resubordinated does not have to know or be able to recognise Colonel Popovic because he still receives assignments from his own commander and he executes these assignments. I asked what had happened. He didn't want to answer. What was I supposed to do? Press him? And then I also forgot this: That unit that came had its own security organ because I didn't know those people. How could I investigate? That was supposed to be done by the security organ of that unit. I tried to find out what had happened. The man didn't want to tell me. And that was it. I went on my way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, a witness Dr. Karadzic just called, Tomo Kovac, explained that all these crimes were strictly in your purview, that it was the security organ of the VRS who is meant to investigate them because they were -- the police units, the special police brigade under Borovcanin had been resubordinated. You're now telling us that the security organ of the VRS is not supposed to investigate crimes by the MUP because Tomo Kovac is supposed to do it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Not Tomo Kovac. Why Tomo Kovac? That unit has its own commander. In terms of structure, it was established, was set up like any other VRS unit. It has its own commander, it has its own battalions and companies, company commanders, its assistant commander for security, and he is the one who knows the people. How could I intervene when I don't know the men? Every unit has its --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, you're --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: -- own commanders. They're all set up in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. You explained that. So you as the security chief for the Drina Corps, when you stumble across a pile of bodies and a unit that is resubordinated to the Drina Corps, are unable to gather any information; that's what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: That's not right. I said I had asked what had happened. The man didn't want to share information with me because he didn't know me. To him, I was a stranger. He knows his own men, his own company commander, his security commander. Who is Popovic to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I can produce my ID to him a hundred times; it still won't mean anything to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So as a law-abiding, Geneva-Convention-abiding VRS officer who doesn't approve of mass murder, you would have immediately then called up Ljubisa Borovcanin and said: What the hell's going on, your men are standing around a bunch of dead bodies in front of a warehouse. You need to go and investigate this now. Right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if everybody is monitoring their own unit and he is duty-bound to do so, then he must take responsibility for his own unit. I tried to find out what had happened; I didn't get an answer. I went on my way and then made inquiries at the command about what had happened. However, the staff of the command, the senior staff, was not there. There was only auxiliary personnel, but I did try to do something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, did you try to do this, because there's nothing in your statement: What did you to check on whether there were any survivors? What did you do to check whether any of these men lying on the ground or in the warehouse might still have been alive and in great pain? When you got to Bratunac did you say: I think we should send some ambulances to Kravica, there's a whole people lying on the ground who have been shot and there might be some who are alive?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you I was watching from the road, and what I saw I described to you. When I came to the command, I tried to find out what had happened. Nobody was able to tell me more than I already knew, and I didn't take the steps that you suggest. I didn't take steps because I thought after all it was the responsibility of the person in command of that unit. I cannot interfere in the command and the operation of another unit. Everybody has their own security organ. I cannot -- I mean, I can send instructions to them along my own chain of command as to how they should work, but nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. The road is very close to the Kravica warehouse and the Trial Chamber's been there. You keep saying you were on the road. It's right there, it's right off the road; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: On the road itself, if I remember correctly, there was a green belt between the road and the wire fence, and then another green belt, then a paved area outside the warehouse and then the warehouse itself. It was a minimum of 20-plus, 20 to 30 metres, as far as I'm able to estimate now from memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And just before we finish today, when you came across those bodies and you saw that scene, were you emotionally shaken? Did you start to cry like you did at the Bisina execution site?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, it's never a normal thing to see dead bodies in a heap, although they were not in a heap, they were just lying outside the hangar. I was in a section of the road that was a bit wider and I was looking diagonally towards the hangar, and of course when you see something like that, when you come across ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, the evidence in this case - and I think we're about to stop so I'll just put this to you - the evidence in this case from the very few people who survived those executions that day is that in that warehouse there were people moaning and dying all night long. People, if we believe any part of your story, you could have saved.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, at that moment when I was passing by, I was standing by my car, I didn't hear a thing. The engine was running. I called out to the man who was 10, 15 metres away from me and asked him: What's happened? He said: An incident, and waved me off. I didn't hear any cries.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 109, lines 21 and 22 do not reflect exactly what the witness says. [In English] I can send the instructions to them along my chain of command as to how they should work, but nothing else. [Interpretation] The witness actually said [In English] But to nobody else. [Interpretation] He didn't say "nothing else," but he said he can only send instructions down his own chain of command but not send instructions to anyone else. And that is also not quite correctly interpreted. Only along our chain to my own subordinates. In our language the two can be confused easily. There's only one sound distinguishing the two words, but he actually said "to no one else."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. There's not much difference as far as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I ask one more questions before we break based on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, okay, then you're at the Bratunac Brigade after seeing these bodies and recall there was a Bratunac Brigade soldier who was wounded at this site, at this execution site on the 13th. You could have gone to your subordinate chain right then and said: Get out to Kravica and find out what happened. There's a whole bunch of dead bodies lying at the warehouse. I saw them from the road. But you didn't.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, at that moment, I did not know at that moment that a soldier, any soldier, had been hurt. All I knew, all I heard, was that an incident had happened. When I came to the command, I made inquiries at the command if anybody knew what had happened back there. However, I didn't find any senior officers who would be able to tell me anything. Maybe even they didn't know anything about it at the moment. I don't know whether I would have or should have done otherwise if I had learned more, but I was simply unable to find anyone who would give me more information. All I was told was that something had happened, which means that the information didn't reach anyone on time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. Nicholls kindly make it clear whether he means the policemen or the soldier because the interpretation we got was "soldier."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also received interpretation "soldier."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Soldier, VRS soldier. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether it was a soldier who was wounded at that site, that was the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, soldier, VRS soldier, Bratunac Brigade soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A Bratunac soldier was wounded in the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's the challenge -- question from --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm confirming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It was not an error, soldier, not policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like to answer -- would you like to comment on that, Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I didn't know a soldier was hurt. I thought as I was passing by that a policeman had been injured. As for a soldier ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we adjourn or would you like to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think we can -- if I'm right, we're past the time. We can continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Popovic, I'd like to advise you not to discuss about your testimony with anybody else. I take it you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, sorry, just to make it clear, does that include his attorney because you made the similar ruling with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- Mr. Kovac that he could speak to his lawyer but not about the case, not about his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Mr. Zivanovic, you understand. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 6th day of November, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.50 p.m.,
